## MAXIMILIAN,
### Arch-Steward of the Holy Roman Empire, Elector;

->And to his Most Serene consort,<-
## ELISABETH,
### Counts Palatine of the Rhine, Dukes of the Bavarians;
<note>The Latin "Bojorum" refers to the Boii, an ancient tribe from whom the name Bavaria is derived.</note>

->To my most Merciful Lords.<-

Human affections vary wonderfully, Most Serene Princes, in the pursuit of virtues. There are those who devote themselves solely to *Patience*, a virtue necessary for all things. They do well and wisely. Others raise *Obedience* to the throne, and say that it holds the greatest authority over the entire company of virtues. These too do not act wrongly. There are those who call the foundation of a holier life *Humility* <note>original: "Demissionem animi," literally a lowering of the mind or spirit.</note>. And these also do well. Many hail *Justice* as the foremost virtue. Learnedly so. Others make *Charity* the queen over all virtues: What

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE

...better? Now truly, concerning the path by which each of those individual virtues is to be reached, opinions again differ, and the instructions are almost countless. To me, Demetrius the philosopher <note>Demetrius the Cynic (c. 1st century AD), a philosopher famous for his teachings on simplicity and virtue, often cited by Seneca.</note>—a great man of that age, even when compared to the greatest—seems to have spoken most excellently:

<margin>Seneca, Book 7 of *On Benefits*, Chapter 1</margin>
> *It is more beneficial if you hold a few precepts, provided those are ready and in use for you, than if you have indeed learned many things but do not have them at hand.*

It is exactly so: what need is there for many instructions when one suffices? If it is permitted to leap into heaven from a corner, what need is there for so many steps?

This was my reason, Most Serene Dukes, why for several years now—your Serenities having offered most attentive ears to these sacred matters—I have recommended nothing so much as this one thing:

-> T O &nbsp;&nbsp; W I L L &nbsp;&nbsp; W H A T <-
-> G O D &nbsp;&nbsp; W I L L S. <-
<note>original: "VELLE QUOD VULT DEUS." This is the core spiritual maxim of the author's work, emphasizing total resignation to Divine providence.</note>

I knew indeed that this could be understood by no one better than by those who have long since experienced it.

<summary>The author argues that practicing one essential spiritual principle is better than knowing many, citing the philosopher Demetrius. He introduces his core teaching to the Dukes of Bavaria: the act of aligning one's will entirely with the will of God.</summary>

### TO THE PRINCES.

But because not all listeners share the same state of mind, nor are they all equally capable of understanding, it seemed advantageous that what was spoken should be reinforced by what is written. This is the purpose of this little book, which hastens toward Your Serenities for this very reason: so that what other listeners could only know and understand through my spoken words, they might also learn to put into practice through the examples of such great Princes. In this way, what were once merely words might become actions.

This is the goal of the *Conforming* <note>original: "Conformatio"—the process of shaping or aligning the human soul to match the Divine pattern.</note> of the human will to the divine. It gently teaches us to always remain flexible in either direction: to desire everything that God desires, and to reject everything that He rejects. In this single precept lies the entirety of wisdom in both divine and human law. By this rule, the works of a lifetime must be arranged; according to this law, anyone who loves more than just a superficial <term>perfunctoriam</term> <note>From the Latin *perfunctorius*, meaning a duty performed merely for the sake of form or appearances, without deep commitment.</note> piety should both perform and measure all their actions.

Where this most holy blending of the human and divine will exists, there the inseparable... <note>The sentence concludes on the following page.</note>

### EPISTLE

...that companionship of all the virtues. Plato defines happiness in more than one place as *Likeness to God* <note>original: "Dei Assimilationem"—the philosophical concept of *homoiosis theo*, or becoming as much like God as is humanly possible through virtue and wisdom.</note>. Let the very words of Plato, worthy of being written in gold, be recorded here in this cheaper ink: <margin>Plato in the *Philebus*, and elsewhere.</margin> *Evil necessarily surrounds and clings to this mortal nature and this lower place. Therefore, one must strive to flee from here to there as quickly as possible: yet this flight is* LIKENESS TO GOD, *as far as is possible.* 

But who is more like God than one who subjects his own will in all things to the divine will? Such a person now desires nothing less than that which he feels he most greatly desires <note>The author implies that the person's own desires have been replaced by God's desires.</note>, being most intent on this one thing: to perform all actions according to the plumb-line <note>original: "perpendiculum"—a lead weight used by masons to ensure a wall is perfectly vertical; here used as a metaphor for the absolute standard of God's will.</note> of the divine will. Whoever has learned this one thing has mastered all useful and necessary knowledge. This science instructs how each person should conduct themselves wisely in times of doubt, in times of adversity, and in times of joy: so that they may handle uncertainty with prudence, adversity with fortitude, and joy with moderation...

<summary>The author uses Plato’s definition of happiness as "likeness to God" to argue that the highest form of wisdom is the total submission of the human will to the Divine. He describes this alignment as a "science" that provides the moral foundation for navigating all of life's challenges.</summary>

...treats you. He whose life is in harmony with the will of God <note>original: "voluntate Dei"</note> despises all chance accidents, raises himself above every fear, and consecrates his soul to virtue. Wherever virtue calls, he finds the path level; he stands always on solid and serene ground. As often as he wishes, he takes part in heaven; nor can he ever be so wretched that he does not breathe most sweetly in the bosom of God. 

Just as craftsmen, if they tire their eyes by focusing intently on some delicate task, step out into the open and refresh their weary sight with the free light and air: so the soul, though locked in this somber dwelling-place of the body, seeks the open whenever it wishes and rests in the contemplation of the divine will with a most holy delight. This delight is steady and fearless, never to feel weariness of itself. Here is solid security and unshakable confidence. He who has surrendered himself entirely to the divine will has reached the very summit of human good.

And this is the unique aspect of wisdom <margin>the will of God, virtue, soul, contemplation, wisdom</margin>

# DEDICATORY LETTER

The teaching is handed down in these five books, which I lay down at your feet, Most Serene Princes, as if at the altar of Clemency <note>original: "Clementiæ aram" — A metaphor suggesting the Princes' mercy and kindness are like a sacred sanctuary</note>. Before now, I committed to your most serene hands my *Considerations on ETERNITY*. To those, it was necessary to add the *RIGHT INTENTION*, which serves as the Rule <term>Amuſſis: A mason’s level or ruler used to ensure perfect alignment; here used to mean an exacting moral standard</term> of human actions. This was to be followed in proper order by the CONFORMITY of the human will with the divine. The goal of human life is *Eternity*. Toward this goal, *Right Intention* leads the way. But truly, the most exact pattern of *Right Intention* is *To Will what God wills* <note>original: "Velle quod vult Deus"</note>, and to do so in all things. 

In this way, the specific parts were to be joined to their general category. And these little writings—rough and unpolished in their style, I confess, but to be valued for the subject matter to which they point as if with a finger—I gladly and most deservedly consecrate to Your Serene Highnesses by every right and title. For this one thing alone almost remains for me: To wish not to be ungrate-

<meta>This page begins the preface "To the Reader" following the dedication to the Princes of Bavaria. The catchword "rum" from the previous page likely concluded the word "gratissimum" or "ingratum" in the Latin dedication, which was translated in the previous segment.</meta>

# TO THE READER.

HERE is for you, my best Reader, the most solid foundation (I say this boldly) of all virtues. I have chosen to call it *The Heliotrope* <note>original: "Heliotropium" — a flower, such as the sunflower or turnsole, that turns to follow the sun. Drexel uses it as a metaphor for the human soul following God.</note>, a name which I judge to be most convenient and appropriate for this subject. The Heliotrope is a herb very well known in pharmacies; it turns its head with such strict devotion <note>original: "religione" — here meaning a natural, fixed instinct or duty</note> toward every movement of the sun that it never fails to look toward it, even when the sun is covered by clouds; for this reason, they have named it the "Bride of the Sun." The human will, if it does not wish to go astray, must balance itself at every moment and toward every nod of the divine will, just as the Heliotrope balances itself toward its own Sun. And this is that unconquerable wisdom; this is the firm and impenetrable shield against all adversity: **TO WILL WHAT GOD WILLS.** I believe this teaching—of conforming the human will to the divine—is the summary <note>original: "epitomen"</note> of all the sacred volumes and the shorthand <note>original: "compendium"</note> of all holiness. Whoever has learned to subject his own will to the divine will already understands the entire Bible.

But I should warn you of this early on: in such a serious matter, one should not get stuck on petty words. "Conformity of the human will with the divine," "Resignation of oneself to the divine pleasure," "Union of the human and divine wills," etc.—these are essentially the same thing, differing only in name. Grant me pardon, Reader, and dare not to be offended by words that are not quite pure Latin <note>Drexel is apologizing for using technical theological or "Scholastic" Latin terms rather than the polished classical Latin of ancient Rome</note>. My intention is to speak here with the many, and to bring the secret of the divine will into the light, not to hide it behind wordy—

<note>The text ends mid-word "verbo-" (likely "verbositate" or "wordiness"), to be continued on the following page.</note>

<vocab>Heliotrope, human will, divine will, wisdom, holiness, Bible, conformity, resignation, union of wills</vocab>

<summary>Jeremiah Drexel introduces his work by using the Heliotrope flower as a metaphor for how the human soul should constantly turn toward the will of God. He argues that conforming one's will to God's is the essence of all Christian teaching and the ultimate spiritual shield.</summary>
<keywords>Heliotrope, divine will, spiritual discipline, conformity, Jeremiah Drexel, Christian ethics, Jesuit spirituality</keywords>

# TO THE READER.

<meta>catchword: This</meta>

...[wordy] wrappings: <note>The Latin "rum involucris" suggests the end of a sentence about not getting lost in "wordy coverings" or flowery language.</note> these have been written as a remedy for the soul, not as an exercise of the mind. Indeed, I believe that many of my works have already reached your hands. There have preceded:

**Eternity**, *Considerations on*.
**The Christian Zodiac**, *or, the twelve signs of Predestination*.
**The Clock** *of the Guardian Angel*.
**Nicetas**, *or, Unchastity Triumphed Over*.
**Trismegistus** <note>original: "Trismegistus" — literally "thrice-greatest," a name usually associated with the mythical Hermes Trismegistus, but here used as a title for a work on spiritual mastery.</note>, *on Conscience, the Veneration of the Saints, and the Care of the Body*.
**Right Intention**, *the Mason’s Rule <note>original: "Amussis" — a tool used by builders to ensure a surface is perfectly flat; a metaphor for a precise standard of behavior.</note> of all actions*. Now follows
**The Heliotrope**, *or*, the **Conforming** *of the human will to the divine*.

I consider this last work to be the Sum and Compendium of all the previous ones, and indeed of all the virtues combined. However, he will best understand this work who has already seen the earlier ones. **Right intention** leads toward **God**; but the **Conforming** of the human will to the divine (if I may say so) introduces one into the very heart of God. And see, my Reader, how short and how easy is the path that leads you to a blessed eternity! It is described entirely in these few little words: **TO WILL WHAT GOD WILLS.** This is the whole journey from earth to heaven. Do you wish to ascend there from here? This is the path by which you arrive. You might travel by other ways, but you will never arrive. And I ask you, do not let these words seem to be spoken at too great a length. Here the foundation is laid for every virtue; here the entrance is blocked to all vices. Examine what you read, and you will find the very summit of wisdom in these pages.

<summary>In this preface, Drexel lists his previous spiritual treatises and introduces "The Heliotrope" as his most essential work, centered on the simple principle of aligning one's will with God's.</summary>

### TO THE READER.

<meta>catchword: IMAGE</meta>

**WILLS**.

This one thing I would now kindly advise you, my Reader: when you are ill at ease and do not wish to read much, I would have you at least obtain this for yourself: look into the first chapter of the first book, and the last chapter of the fifth (or final) book. Read through only one part of those chapters on a single day, and I would almost dare to promise that it will be better for your malady <note>original: "morbo" — likely referring to both physical sickness and spiritual or emotional distress.</note>. All those things which seem like evils to others will grow mild for you and turn toward the good, if you learn to rise above them by embracing the **divine will**. In this way, my Reader, listen to God, as one who is himself worthy to be heard.

### A brief explanation of the
### following image.

No one will conform themselves well to the divine will unless they have first understood it well. *We represent the knowledge of the divine will in this way: Saul, thrown to the ground by Christ and now eager to know the divine will, says: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" <note>original: "Domine, quid me vis facere?" — St. Paul’s words at his conversion in Acts 9:6.</note> But Christ sends him to Ananias, who is to explain the divine will to him. For this is indeed how God is accustomed to act: He teaches men the secret of His will, but He does so through other men.*

Here, moreover, we establish a double symbol of both the human and divine will. 1. *A heart crowned with a golden wreath, surrounded by a lily and a sword,* signifies the WILL OF GOD, which restrains its own people through both reward <note>symbolized by the lily and crown</note> and punishment <note>symbolized by the sword</note>. I am watchful for every nod of yours." <note>original: "nutus" — refers to a command given by a simple gesture, implying total obedience to the slightest sign.</note>

When Alexander, the Macedonian King, was pursuing Darius in war, he became overheated by the sun and the intensity of the march. He plunged his body into the river Cydnus <note>The Cydnus river was famous for its icy waters, even in the height of summer.</note>, but his limbs suddenly grew numb with a chill, and he was carried into his tent looking like a dying man. Once his friends and physicians had been admitted, the King told them it would be better for him to die bravely than to recover slowly. Therefore, if there were any help or medical skill available, they should know that he was seeking a remedy not so much for death as for the war <note>original: "non tam mortis quam belli remedium" - Alexander was more concerned with returning to his campaign than his personal survival.</note>.

When they had settled their opinion on a single potion, Philip the physician—who had been assigned to the King since his youth as a most faithful companion and guardian of his health—promised to bring a remedy that was not reckless but vigorous. **I.** The chief point of all the doctrine which Christ handed down in so many most divine sermons was this: to conform oneself entirely and perfectly to the divine will in all things, both great and small. <margin>At least by a secondary intention.</margin>
(...and, as they say in the schools, effectively and positively) <note>original: "effective positive." These are technical scholastic terms meaning God acts directly and purposefully to bring about a result, rather than just letting it happen.</note> God wills all evils of punishment and nature for the most just of causes; He only permits sin, or guilt. For this reason, the latter is called God's **Permitting Will**, while the former is called His **Ordaining Will**. <term>Permitting vs. Ordaining Will: A theological distinction. God "permits" human sin to preserve free will, but He "ordains" or actively directs natural events and the consequences of sin (punishments) to maintain cosmic justice.</term> Therefore, everything that we call "evil" comes from the will of God. So say the theologians. ### III.
In this matter, many people deceive themselves through a wretched ignorance. They convince themselves that only those evils arising from natural causes—such as floods, earthquakes, the barrenness of fields, landslides, the <term>high cost of grain<note>original: "annonae caritas." This refers to inflation or scarcity of food, which was a frequent cause of social unrest and famine in the 17th century.</note></term>, harsh weather, the distress of diseases, and death—are sent by God, especially since human sin usually plays no role in causing them.

However, they believe that those evils stemming from human vice and malice—such as slanders, frauds, thefts, harassments, plots, injuries, robberies, oppressions, wars, and slaughters—are not from God, nor do they proceed from His providence, but rather from the wickedness of men and the perverse will of those who plot such things against others. 

From this mindset come those cries heard everywhere in recent years: “This high cost of grain is not from God; it comes from the greediest of men, it is not from God!” These are insane and impious voices, utterly unworthy of a Christian, and fit to be banished to the <note>original: "sub orcum relegandæ" — literally "banished to the underworld."</note> depths of hell.

But to make this matter perfectly clear, let us demonstrate what we are saying with an example. Suppose there is someone who wishes another to be stripped of all his possessions:

God is not the author or cause of this <insert>evil</insert>, although He permitted this plan to be undertaken. For He could have hindered this if He had wished. Since, therefore, God in His just judgment did not hinder that impious plan, He permitted it. We will provide the reasons for this permission below.

For the <term>Will of the Sign<note>original: "voluntas Signi." A theological term referring to God's will as expressed through His revealed commands, laws, and prohibitions—what He tells us we *should* do.</note></term> (to speak as the theologians do) is one thing, and the <term>Will of His Good Pleasure<note>original: "voluntas Beneplaciti." And regarding that Will of the Sign, explained to us through the laws, it is for the most part quite clear; but regarding this Will of Good Pleasure, it is not the same, nor is it immediately possible to know how far it extends. I shall discuss this more fully below. 

Now, let us take *Illness* as an example. From whatever cause it arises, it is according to the divine will, and there is no room for doubt in this matter. However, since a sick person does not know how long God wishes him to lie in bed with the disease, he may lawfully resist it and apply whatever lawful <term>remedies<note>original: "remedia." Referring to medical treatments or medicines.</note></term> exist for recovering his health. But when he has tried everything and nothing has succeeded, nor has he recovered, he should be fully convinced that it is the divine will for him to be burdened by a more serious and lasting illness. Thus, one must reason in this way: “God wants you, my sick friend, to be ill; but because you do not know whether He also wants you never to be healed, for that reason you lawfully use remedies; if, however...”

Therefore, those of a crooked heart (says Augustine), that is, the distorted of heart, hold three opinions: Either there is no God—for "the fool has said in his heart, there is no God" <note>A reference to Psalm 14:1.</note>—or God is unjust because these things please Him and He does them; or God does not govern human affairs, nor does He care for any of us. In these three opinions lies great impiety.

### CHAPTER II.

*What, how, and why the Will of God permits this or that.*

The common people are prone to wander into a wretched error here; to them, **Divine Permission** <term>Permissio divina: The theological concept of God "allowing" an event to happen without being the moral cause of a sin.</term> is hardly different from human permission, which sits idle and does nothing, failing to stop those who wish to act even when it has the power to do so. From this single error, innumerable evils are born. Because of it, we rush at one another, and as if we were the makers of every misfortune and the authors of every evil, we tear each other apart with words, hands, and teeth—as if God, in the meantime, were watching our disputes idly and permitting the gravest injuries despite being able to prevent them. This is the breeding ground <note>original: "seminarium," literally a nursery or seed-plot.</note> of all spiritual disturbances. To overturn this, we have established three main points to be considered in every instance of Divine Permission.

The first is the **Will to Permit**; the second, the **cause of the Permission**; the third, the **Co-operating Will** <term>Voluntas Cooperatrix: The concept that God provides the "power" for an action to exist, even if the human "will" directs that action toward a sinful end.</term> in the thing permitted. To see these more clearly, we must recall to mind that there are two kinds of evils. The first are those that bring trouble, pain, loss, and infamy—such as poverty, imprisonment, disease, exile, and death—which should not be called "evils" so much as **bitter medicines** applied by the divine hand. The second kind of evils are those that are truly called "evils" by name, such as sins.

...afflicted. God truly wills those former things <note>The "former things" refers to the "evils of pain" (trouble, loss, etc.) mentioned on the previous page.</note>, either for the punishment of the wicked, as Augustine says, or for the discipline of His children. However, of these latter things <note>Referring to "evils of guilt" or sins.</note>, God should not be said to "will" them, but rather to permit them. Since God truly wills all things that truly exist—for by His will all things are, and without His will nothing is—He cannot "will" sin (which is improperly said to "exist" <note>In traditional theology, sin is defined as a "privation" or a lack of good, much like darkness is the absence of light; therefore, it has no "being" of its own for God to create.</note>), but only permit it.

Just as God most perfectly foresees all future things, so too can He most easily hinder whatever He wishes. However, since He does not hinder countless things, it must be said that God, by His most just will, has willed from eternity and thus decreed to permit them. God, certainly, allows something to happen not because He is unwilling, but because He is willing. Men, indeed, permit many things which they either cannot hinder, or certainly would prefer did not happen. Not so with the supreme Arbiter of all things. There is, therefore, in God a *Will to Permit* <term>Voluntas Permittendi: The theological idea that God's "allowing" of an event is a deliberate choice, not a lack of power.</term>, which we established as the first heading in our study of Permission. Here the question is asked: why did God will to permit sins? Or rather, what is the cause of this permission in God?

I. Certainly, that infinite Goodness would never permit such great malice in the world unless He drew greater goods from it, and turned things intended for destruction toward salvation. God permitted the envy of brothers to rage against the innocent Joseph, but for how great a good did He permit it—not only for his parents and brothers, but for all of Egypt? <header>BOOK I.</header>

...[He permitted] Saul to be driven by the most serious injustices, but for the greatest good of David and the entire Hebrew kingdom <note>King Saul’s persecution of David ultimately prepared David to be a wiser king and fulfilled God's plan for the lineage of Israel.</note>. God permitted Daniel, most unjustly accused, to be cast into the abyss of the lions, but for the great good of Daniel himself and of many others. But why do I recount these things? Thus, indeed, from every divine permission, the greatest increases of divine glory and the most abundant benefits for the human race arise. From this, the Goodness of God and His Mercy, from this His Generosity and Power, from this His Providence, and from this His Wisdom and Justice shine forth in an utterly admirable way: from this the virtue of many grows, struggles are sought after, rewards are multiplied, and crowns <note>The "crown" refers to the "crown of life" or "crown of glory," a traditional Christian symbol for the spiritual reward of the faithful after death.</note> are increased.

And how admirable divine Providence shows itself in these daily permissions! For what great thing is it if you make good from good? But it is a very great thing if you have made good from evil. On a calm sea, as they say, anyone is a pilot <note>original: "gubernator." This refers to the steersman or captain of a ship.</note>. <margin>*Seneca, Letter 85*</margin> Nor indeed is it a matter of great skill to keep the harbor in sight when the wind is favorable, the ship is sturdy, the sea is peaceful, the stars are helpful, and the rowers are most experienced; but to reach the desired harbor nonetheless while winds struggle against each other, the vessel is torn, the sky roars, pirates lie in wait, the rowers are unskilled, and the stars are snatched away—this, finally, is a feat to be admired in a pilot.

-># ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL<-

...it is marvelous. Such is God in His permissions. Through those things which seem contrary, He leads to a happy outcome; through so many crimes of men, He spreads His glory; in such heaps of wicked deeds, He makes His friends more illustrious. With God directing, frauds turn to the advantage of the deceived; harassments and injuries add strength to the one harassed; the impiety of so many ruined men stabilizes the piety of many and preserves them so they do not perish; and from where most are believed to be crushed, they emerge. Joseph’s <note>The biblical Joseph, who was sold into slavery in Egypt by his jealous brothers, eventually became second-in-command to Pharaoh.</note> prison and chains opened the way to such a sublime throne of dignity; his brothers' envy benefited him more than the goodwill of the entire world. Saul's treachery conferred the crown upon David. The lions' den raised Daniel higher than any royal favors could have. From the cross, Christ passed into Paradise; from the Mount of Olives, He reached the session <note>original: "consessum." This refers to the "Session of Christ," the theological concept of Christ ascending to heaven to sit at the right hand of God the Father.</note> of the Father. For if God did not permit sins, and did not order <note>In this context, "to order" (ordinaret) means to arrange or direct events toward a specific end, like a conductor directing an orchestra.</note> those permitted, and by ordering did not derive them into good, we would hardly recognize God's avenging justice. But in this way, we are taught to understand more deeply, and we are forced to confess a most admirable series and connection of causes, through which, at last, so many goods emerge from such great evils. ...for <note>The Latin text begins with "nim," the second half of the word "enim," which started on the previous page.</note> it is right for no human to either grasp with the intellect or explain with speech all the inner workings <note>original: "machinas," literally "machines" or "engines." It should be enough to have perceived this much: that God, the author <note>original: "proditor," meaning the one who brings forth or produces.</note> of all natures, also disposes all things by directing them toward the good. Thus it happens that if you look at the Providence <term>Providence: the protective care of God as a spiritual power that guides the universe.</term> that disposes them, you will realize that there is no evil anywhere among the things believed to be so abundant on earth. Therefore, the reason for divine permission <note>Theological "permission" is the concept that God allows certain things (like suffering or free-willed actions) to happen without being the direct author of the sin involved.</note> is manifold—and this was our second main point.

11. The third point is the **Cooperating Will of God** in every matter which He permits. God did not only decree from eternity what He would permit to occur in the course of time, nor did He only decree the most just reasons for His permission; He also had, and continues to have, a cooperating will in all these permissions. In the schools of the theologians <note>original: "Theologorum scholis." This refers to the academic setting of "Scholasticism," where precise definitions of God's nature and actions were debated.</note>, it is a most certain truth that God is the helper <note>original: "adjutorem." This implies that God provides the "being" or the "power" for an action to happen, even if the human intent behind the action is wrong.</note> of everything that truly occurs and exists. Nothing anywhere exists without the aid of the **first and highest cause** <term>First Cause: a philosophical term for the ultimate origin of all existence—God—upon whom all secondary causes depend.</term>.

Since, therefore, God decreed from eternity to permit all these things, and did so for the most just reasons, and even offers Himself as a helper in His permissions, why is it that we attack God and men with so many vain complaints? Why do we so often bark against Providence and God’s most just permissions? Why do we not rather ascribe all events to divine judgments, certain that the most just and weighty reasons for the divine permission lie beneath them?

### III.

I ask you, my Christian friend—you especially, who so often disturb heaven and earth with your complaints. Tell me, I pray: regarding that man who harmed you, what exactly do you accuse? Is it only his will to do harm, or only his power to do it, or both? "Both," you will say.

But I will teach you to accuse neither. Not the will to harm, for without the power to act, this will is empty and has done you no harm; nor should you accuse the power to harm, which is from God and is just and fair. From this principle, indeed, no man's sin deserves more pardon simply because God draws a greater good from it; for man provides only the <term>occasion|A circumstance that allows something to happen, without being the primary force that causes it</term> of the good, not the cause. Furthermore, he provides that occasion not from himself, but from the abundance of divine goodness. If a wicked man burns down a poor man's hut, he has committed no less a crime just because the poor man bore it patiently, or because some Prince replaced it with a house ten times better. The virtue of another and a fortunate outcome do not wash away the arsonist's guilt; likewise, sin acquires no goodness of its own just because it provided the occasion for a good result. But so that we may better understand all these things, we must now consider how hidden the judgments of God are.

...of God’s servants, the will of God is to be recognized in all things. Here we will provide several rules through which the divine will can be easily explored.

->*For recognizing the divine will.*<-

Whatever leads away from God is against God’s will; whatever invites one toward God is according to the divine will. For this is the will of God: your sanctification <note>In this context, sanctification refers to the process of being made holy or set apart for God's purposes.</note>, that you should abstain from fornication, etc. Therefore, if anyone detects such a factor in themselves that they are forced to admit: "This duty, this social circle, this trade <note>original: "mercimonium"; refers to one's business or commercial dealings.</note>, this way of life does not make me holier; I am being led away from God, albeit gradually and with slow steps," then neither that duty, nor that society, nor that trade, nor that way of life is according to the divine will.

### II. Rule.

The will of God is most clearly declared to us through the law of God and of the Church. Therefore, in every moment of ambiguity, one must not only ask what the laws of God or the Church require, but what is more or less conformed to them. Long ago, when a wealthy young man asked which was the nearest way to heaven, Christ pointed to this best interpreter of the divine will, saying: "You know the commandments?" <note>Referring to the story of the Rich Young Ruler found in the Gospels.</note> Indeed, nothing is sweeter than to look back upon the commandments of the Lord. This very messenger <note>original: "internuncium"; a go-between or intermediary.</note> of the divine will...

Ecclesiasticus 23:37. <note>In modern Bibles, this is often cited as Sirach 23:27, which states that nothing is better than the fear of the Lord and attending to His commandments.</note>

The divine Paul says: "Do not be conformed to this world," etc., "so that you may discern what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God." <note>A reference to Romans 12:2.</note> The **good** will of God is contained in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>; the **pleasing** will in the Gospel counsels <note>Traditionally referring to the "Evangelical Counsels" of poverty, chastity, and obedience which go beyond the basic requirements of the law.</note>; the **perfect** will desires that what He has commanded be fulfilled on earth as it is in heaven.

### III. Rule

<margin>1 Thessalonians chapter 5, verse 17 and following.</margin>
This rule is prescribed by the blessed Paul: "Give thanks in all things; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you." First, it is most worthy of note here that thanks should be given in all matters, even those most turbulent and unsuccessful. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful oratory.</note> beautifully said: <margin>Chrysostom on that passage.</margin> "Have you suffered some evil? If you choose, it is not evil. Give thanks to God, and you have already changed the evil into good." This belongs to a philosophical mind. The ancient Germans used to instruct their children excellently, so that if they ever hurt a finger in the fire, they would immediately say: "Thanks be to God" <note>original: "Deo gratias."</note>. A brief but noble precept. Whatever at last, my Christian friend, presses upon you or burns you, whatever afflicts you, say a hundred times, say a thousand times: **"Thanks be to God."** Paul adds: **"Do not quench the Spirit."** Let there be a place for divine inspirations. Not infrequently, God explains His will through hidden conversations <note>original: "occultis alloquiis"; these are internal spiritual promptings or the "still small voice" of conscience and inspiration.</note>, which are safely believed to be truly divine when the pursuit of God’s glory alone is proposed as the goal.

Beyond the laws of God and the Church, there are also other interpreters of the divine will, especially in doubtful matters. When Saul, already prepared to obey the divine will, had asked: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" the Lord did not weigh him down with commandments, nor did He suddenly pour all knowledge into him. ### V. Rule.

If time or place does not permit one to seek counsel, let a man look within himself; he will be able to resolve all doubt regarding the knowledge of the divine will with ease in the following manner. Let him carefully consider which of the two choices he hesitates between is more acceptable to his own personal will, what is more pleasing to the appetite of the flesh, and what is more desirable for his own reputation. Once he has investigated this—which is an easy task—and has seriously resolved within himself to conform his actions most deeply to the divine will, then he will surely and safely choose that which is less acceptable to his own will, and less pleasing to the appetite of the flesh...

Here, let there be a consolation, such as sometimes happens to a preacher <term>ecclesiastæ</term> [a member of the clergy]. We explain the matter thus: A preacher <term>Concionator</term> [one who delivers a sermon] in the afternoon sees almost all of his listeners sleeping; he is not a little disturbed by so many nodding off at him, yet it seems more tolerable than if as many were shamelessly chattering. Therefore, if two or three do not sleep, he says to himself: "That is enough for me, and there is reason for me to go on; one is as good as thousands." Let a person, however much disturbed, reason no differently: as long as two eyes remain awake—*Reason and Will*—as long as these watchmen observe the will of God, let other things be turned upside down; I indeed shall stand unshaken, and although I may not immediately follow the divine nods <note>original: "nutus" — a gesture of the head, implying God's subtle commands or hints.</note>, I shall nonetheless strive to follow them.

### VI. Rule.

To search out the divine will, it is of great value to ask with Paul: <note>original: "Domine, quid me vis facere?" — This refers to the conversion of St. Paul on the road to Damascus as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles.</note> Lord, what do you want me to do? This is the custom of the Saints: in doubtful and complex matters, to flee to the protection of prayer, just as Moses and Aaron once fled to the Tabernacle of the Covenant. And just as when clouds gather so thickly that the sky begins to thunder and roar, the bells in the towers are rung to scatter the clouds: so whenever the sun of the divine will is withdrawn from our eyes, so that we almost do not know what should be done, the next thing is to strike the gates of heaven with prayers.

<margin>Acts 8, 9, v. 6.</margin>
Thus Saul, caught by a sudden storm in the middle of the fields, exclaims: Lord, what do you want me to do? The most opportune time to repeat this little prayer often is when the heavenly feast is approached and the Lord's body is held on the tongue; then one should ardently repeat: Lord, what do you want me to do? Indeed, every day during the divine service, when the priest lifts the Eucharist <term>Eucharistiam</term> [the consecrated bread, believed by Catholics to be the actual body of Christ] above his head, let this be the most ardent vow of all: Lord, what do you want me to do? It is most advisable for religious men to recite the formula of their vows daily during the Mass <note>original: "sub sacro" — literally "under the sacred [rite]," referring to the Mass.</note>.

There is no doubt that the most merciful God frequently delays the requested help so that He may more abundantly reward more constant prayers and longer-lasting patience. Certainly, such things must often be wrung from many of us like coins from a miser <note>original: "velut ab avaris numi" — a vivid metaphor suggesting that humans are often "stingy" with their spiritual devotion unless God's delay forces them to be more persistent.</note>. God would receive few prayers and even rarer patience from us if He did not stir our sluggishness in this way. And so, it is often most useful for us to have obtained nothing through long-lasting prayers. For the profit of such lengthy prayers is usually greater than the profit of the request being granted would have been. This realization should bring great peace to everyone: that they have offered many prayers, even if those prayers were not ratified.

### VII. Rule.

No mortal discovers the divine will more certainly than he who more sincerely desires to conform himself to it in all things. This desire is truly a **thread** <note>original: "filum" — likely an allusion to Ariadne's thread used to navigate the Cretan labyrinth.</note> for untangling the wanderings of every labyrinth; from this, all ambiguity concerning the divine will is removed. Even if someone should be ignorant of what God wants, or which of two lawful choices He prefers, if he is so disposed in spirit that he can say with the most sincere mind: "Lord, if I knew what You wished for me to do in this matter, I would certainly do it." Once this pledge <term>pledge (sponsione): a solemn promise or inner commitment made to God</term> has been made, let him do freely what he will and cease to trouble himself; he will not easily offend the divine will. 

The most loving Father does not desert such a son, nor does He allow him to wander too far from His will. If there is no man to instruct him, He sends an Angel, just as He sent one to Joseph <note>referring to St. Joseph being guided by angels in dreams regarding Mary and the flight to Egypt.</note> when he was deliberating on a serious matter as to what would be best to do; likewise, to the three **Rulers from the East** <note>original: "tribus ex Oriente Dynastis" — the Three Wise Men or Magi.</note> after they had worshipped the divine Infant in his grassy cradle,

In the year 324, Constantine the Great, having left Rome, began to build a city at Ilium <note>original: "Ilium" — the ancient name for Troy. Constantine originally considered rebuilding Troy before choosing Byzantium.</note>, but because it was the divine will that he should abandon the work he had started and build Byzantium in Thrace instead, God warned him in various ways. For, as Bede and Glycas <note>Michael Glycas was a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian.</note> record, every craftsman’s tool was found the next night on the other shore, transported by a hidden force. In the same place, as Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a Byzantine chronicler and theologian.</note> relates, an eagle picked up a mason’s square <term>mason's square (amussim): a tool used by builders to ensure perfect right angles or level surfaces</term> and dropped it from its talons at Byzantium. Thus, God does not deny the knowledge of His will to those who sincerely seek it.

<margin>Wisdom chapter 1, verse 6. Ecclesiasticus chapter 2, verse 13. <note>In many older Bibles, "Ecclesiasticus" refers to the Book of Sirach.</note></margin>
*The spirit of wisdom is kind* <note>original: "Benignus est spiritus sapientiæ"</note> at this highest level, and most generously imparts itself to all. God is present *to all who seek Him in truth*, and He explains His will with a teaching as wonderful as it is gentle to all those who conduct themselves as disciples here with true submission. We learn to know the will of God best by doing it.

Here we wretched ones often err gravely. We receive the will of God with a most ready affection when it rewards and heaps us with benefits; but when it punishes, we turn away as if it were not God's will—as if people who are ill-disposed toward our safety and reputation had taken counsel to utterly destroy us or severely trouble us, while God was unaware or certainly did not command it. Antiquity told fables of the giants, who attempted to cast down the gods from their stronghold <note>original: "arce" — literally a citadel or fortress. All created things obey not unwillingly, and they listen to that supreme law; yet man, the noblest of creatures, alone kicks back against his Creator and resists.

Why do we feel indignant in vain? All disasters are from God—all of them, all. That a landslide there swallowed some towns is from God’s providence; that a plague elsewhere mowed down many thousands of men is from that same source; that slaughter, war, and tyranny happen both here and there is from that very same providence. But setting aside public matters: when that adversary of yours, my friend, steals a portion of your goods; when that person stains your reputation; when this one harms you in other ways—all of this is from God. He does not only permit it, but He even sends it upon you from heaven; you should know this well: all these things are sent by divine power.

## II. The Will of God

To theologians, the Will of God is twofold. One is the **Will of the Sign** <term>original: *Voluntas Signi* — also known as the "Revealed Will." It is called "of the sign" because God uses signs (like the Ten Commandments or the teachings of Jesus) to show us what He wants us to do</term>, by which God commands, forbids, permits, persuades, or performs something, and He declares this through His laws and precepts. The other is the **Will of Good Pleasure** <term>original: *Voluntas Beneplaciti* — also known as the "Secret" or "Absolute Will." This refers to God’s ultimate plan and what He has determined will actually happen, which humans cannot thwart</term>, by which He wills that something destined should happen in every way, whether with a certain condition or without one. 

He wished to grant eternal happiness to angels and humans, yet on this condition and law: that they themselves did not resist Him by their own free choice. Other things God wills without any such qualification. Just as He willed to create heaven and earth, so He wills that there be a perpetual order and governance of the entire World <note>original: *Orbis* — meaning the universe or the whole created system</note>, through which He arranges all things most wisely. No one can resist this will of God; it submits to no laws, it does nothing by the command of another, and it obeys no one. God Himself affirms this through the prophet Isaiah: 

<margin>
Isaiah chapter 46, verse 10, and chapter 55, verse 11.
</margin>

> My counsel, He says, shall stand, and all my will shall be done. So shall my word be, which shall go forth from my mouth: it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do whatever I have willed. 

We, however, who are but lowly servants, must bear—whether we wish to or not—whatever God has decreed for us from on high. All of us, along with the many-

Augustine explains this excellently: "These," he says, "are the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all His desires; and they are so wisely sought out that when the angelic and human creatures had sinned—that is, they did not do what He willed, but what they themselves willed—He still fulfilled what He willed through that same will of the creature (by which the very thing the Creator did not want was done). He did this by making good use of even evil things, as one who is supremely good." Therefore, although the wicked struggle against the divine will, God nonetheless fulfills His own will through those very people, and uses their worst intentions in the best possible way.

### A brief explanation of the following image.

It is not enough to have recognized the Divine will, unless we embrace it once recognized. Christ taught us this on the Mount of Olives, where he so embraced the cross and the most bitter cup of his Passion: *Father, not my will, but yours be done.* <note>original: *Pater, non mea, ſed tua voluntas fiat* — Luke 22:42</note> The heart of God, or the Divine Will and Providence, constantly urges this upon us: **I AM FOR YOU, YOU ARE FOR ME.** <note>original: *EGO TIBI, TV MIHI*</note> *I am for you by providing in all things, you are for me by serving in all things.* What else should the human will respond here but that royal word? **LET IT BE DONE, LET IT BE DONE.** <note>original: *FIAT, FIAT* — a Latin word meaning "let it happen" or "let it be made," expressing total consent to God’s plan.</note> Must pleasure be abandoned? **LET IT BE DONE, LET IT BE DONE.** Must a loss of money be made? **LET IT BE DONE, LET IT BE DONE.** Must damage to one’s reputation be endured? **LET IT BE DONE, LET IT BE DONE.** Must many adversities be tolerated? **LET IT BE DONE, LET IT BE DONE.** Finally, must one even die? **LET IT BE DONE, LET IT BE DONE** whenever, and in whatever way it shall please God.

The sunflower <term>Heliotropium; literally "sun-turner," a flower used in emblems to represent the soul or the will following the light of God</term> represents this same thing to us; with its face open and upright, it receives the whole sun, and wherever the sun moves itself, that flower turns its head, whether the day be clear or cloudy. Let the human will do the same, and wherever the beckoning of the Divine will calls, there let it go, let it run, let it fly. Do you wish never to go astray? Always follow the Divine Will.

### CHAPTER I.

*The introduction to the <term>conformation</term> <note>The process of shaping or aligning the human soul to match the Divine pattern.</note> of the human will with the divine.*

There was once a <term>theologian</term> <note>original: "Theologus"; a scholar of divinity and sacred scripture.</note> of great renown who, for eight years, pleaded with God in constant prayer to show him a person by whom he might be taught the shortest path to heaven. On that day, therefore, when he was seized by the greatest desire to speak with such a man, and wished for nothing else than to see a master of such secret truth, he seemed to hear a voice brought from heaven which warned him: "Go out to the vestibule of the temple, and you will find the kind of man you seek." He went out, therefore, into the public square, and at the threshold of the holy building he found a beggar with ulcerous legs, flowing with much pus; the beggar's clothing was scarcely worth three obols <note>An ancient Greek coin of very small value; the author uses this to emphasize the man's extreme poverty.</note>. To this man, the theologian wished a bright and prosperous morning. To which the beggar replied: "I do not remember," he said, "that I have ever had a morning that was adverse." At this, the learned man, as if to correct his first greeting, said: "Well then, may God make you fortunate—"

...may God grant it. "But I," said the <term>beggar</term> <note>original: "mendicabulum"; a diminutive form of beggar, often implying someone of very low status or a "poor little beggar."</note>, "have never been unfortunate." The theologian was stunned by this statement, but fearing he might have misheard, he repeated his wish, though in slightly different words: "What is this you say?" he asked, "I am bidding you to be happy." Soon the beggar replied again: "I have never," he said, "been unhappy."

The theologian, thinking the clever beggar was splitting hairs or being witty, and wanting to test the man's character, said: "I wish that the things you desire may happen to you, and let it be done." "There is nothing," said the man, "for me to complain about here: All things happen as I wish; although I do not concern myself with the designs of <term>Fortune</term> <note>original: "fortunae"; referring to the classical concept of chance or luck personified as a fickle goddess.</note>." 

But that doctor, greeting him again or perhaps bidding him farewell, said: "May God preserve you, good man, if you indeed have such little regard for fortune. But tell me, I pray, are you the only blessed soul among calamitous mortals? Was Job then mistaken, who asserted: *'Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries'* <note>A direct reference to the Vulgate Bible, Job 14:1, emphasizing the human condition of suffering.</note>? And how have you alone escaped all evil days? I do not fully grasp the meaning of your mind."

To which the beggar replied: "It is as I said, my Lord. When you wished me a prosperous morning, I denied that I had ever had an unprosperous one. I am most content with my lot, which God has assigned to me here. Not needing happiness is my happiness. Those monsters, Fortune and Misfortune, harm no one except the one who is willing, or certainly the one who fears to be harmed. Nor do I ever pray to fortune, but to the Heavenly Father, who governs the outcomes of all things. Thus, I have never been unhappy..."

<summary>In this dialogue, the beggar explains his radical contentment, arguing that because he aligns his will with God's providence, he is immune to the "misfortunes" of chance. He challenges the theologian's traditional understanding of suffering by claiming that true happiness is found in not needing worldly success.</summary>

# BOOK II.

...[unprosperous] I have been, I say, as one to whom all things fall out according to my wish. But if I am pressed by hunger, I praise God as a most provident father for it. If cold burns me, if a storm rushes upon me, if the sky attacks me with other injuries, I praise God equally; when I am a mockery to others, I praise God no less. For I am certain that God is the author of all these things, and that what God does cannot but be the best. Therefore, whatever God either grants or permits to happen, whether it be pleasing or displeasing, sweet or bitter, I hold as the same; for I joyfully accept all these things as if from the hand of the best parent, and I wish this one thing: what God wishes; thus all things happen as I wish.

He is miserable who believes that <term>Fortune</term> <note>The beggar contrasts Fortune (chance/luck) with Divine Providence. To him, Fortune is an illusion; everything is actually directed by God.</note> has any power over him, and he indeed is truly unhappy who dreams of some unknown happiness in this world. This is true happiness in this life: to cling most tenaciously to the divine will alone. God's will is the best, most upright will, which cannot become more upright, nor can it be evil; this will judges all things, but nothing judges it. To follow this, I apply all my effort; I lean into this one care with my whole mind: that whatever God wishes, I also may never fail to wish. For that reason, I by no means consider myself unhappy, since I have poured my entire will so completely into the divine will that, for me, there is no other **To Will** or **Not to Will** <note>original: *Velle* or *Nolle*. These Latin infinitives are used here as nouns to describe the very faculty of choice and desire.</note> than what God wishes or does not wish.

"Is it truly so?" said the <term>Theologian</term>, "do you speak these things from your heart's conviction..."

### III. *The Cheerful Will*. 
This instructs a person to be entirely content both with their food and with all other things which they receive daily as if from the hand of God. Such a person says: "My Lord, whatever You give me is enough, even if to my greed it might sometimes seem too little; I have not earned any of it in any way; You are excessively generous toward me. Indeed, I feel myself unworthy even of the very air I breathe."

A student of the divine will is never accustomed to complain; no one will hear such things from him as: "I can hardly make a living for myself, while others live most sumptuously and do not take on even half of my labor; they endure little, yet they gather the most abundant harvests." V. *Burning Will*. This consists in a person not only wanting or not wanting what God wants or does not want, but for the sake of this very *Not Willing* or *Willing* of God, they reject the one and admit the other with burning zeal. Such a person should have no other cause for doing this or omitting that than the divine pleasure. <margin>For Isaiah was killed in the year of the World 3340.</margin> <note>The "Year of the World" (*Anno Mundi*) is a dating system based on the biblical account of creation. He has arranged, with the greatest clarity and order, the time when each person is to be born and when they are to die; he has prepared every aid for us to reach <term>blessedness</term> <note>The Latin *beatitudo* refers to the ultimate state of spiritual fulfillment and peace in the presence of God.</note>; he foresaw what each of us would think, say, and do throughout our entire lives, and in what way we would accept the help he offered.

### How the human will is to be conformed to the will of God.

We have spoken of what preparation must come before this joining of wills, and which human will can be considered most fit for conformity with the divine; now we must further discuss how, in actual practice, the will of man is to be conformed to the will of God.

I. Thomas Aquinas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was a preeminent philosopher and theologian. He argued that the morality of an action depends heavily on the intention behind it.</note> very rightly said that all actions associated with <term>virtue</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to moral excellence and the habitual disposition to do good.</note> are approved by God for this reason: if they are done with the intention of obeying the divine will. It is of no merit even to pour out one's life and blood, unless it is according to the pleasure of the divine will. The holy man Pæmen <note>Poemen (c. 340–450 AD) was an influential "Desert Father" in Egypt, whose sayings were collected as guides for spiritual life.</note> advised this constantly, saying: "Never set your own will against the divine; let your will always be most closely joined to the divine." If this union is true, it is a most sincere harmony with the divine will in all things, which so instructs a person that these words are constantly on their lips: "As God wills, so also do I; when it is pleasing to God, then it is pleasing to me too."

### BOOK II ###

...will be done, but yours. There is no better, nor almost shorter prayer; there is none more perfect, more pleasing to God, nor more useful to man than this single one: *Not my will, but yours be done*; *Not as I will, but as you will.* Let God’s will be done, even if the world falls. <note>original: "Dei voluntas fiat, etsi Orbis ruat." This is a spiritual variation of the famous Latin legal maxim "fiat justitia ruat caelum"—let justice be done though the heavens fall.</note> Blessed Gertrude <note>Gertrude the Great (1256–1302) was a German Benedictine nun and mystic known for her devotion to the Sacred Heart.</note> was accustomed to say three hundred and sixty-three times: "O my most beloved **Jesus**, your will be done." But we will advise on this more fully below.

<margin>Cassian, *Conferences*, book 9, chapter 20.</margin>
Cassian <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435) was a monk and theologian whose writings brought the wisdom of the Egyptian Desert Fathers to the Western world.</note> says: "What else is it to say, *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven*, than to pray that men may be like Angels? And just as God's will is fulfilled by them in heaven, so also may those who are on earth do not their own will, but the will of the Almighty. Furthermore, no one will be able to say this from the heart except the one who believes that God manages all things we see—whether adverse or prosperous—for our benefit, and that He is more provident and concerned for the safety and interests of His own than we are for ourselves." Thus, in Cassian’s view, he who matches his own will to the divine already dwells in the vestibule of heaven. Certainly, in heaven, countless thousands of the blessed are of one single will. Because of this, Arsenius <note>Arsenius the Great (c. 350–445) was a high-ranking Roman tutor who abandoned the imperial court to live as a hermit in Egypt.</note> replied aptly to Abbot Marcus when he asked: "Why, Father, do you not visit us?" He answered: "I get along better with those who dwell above us, since they all desire the same thing; among men, however, there is almost as much difference in their wills as there is in their faces."

Do you not knit your brow, O Christian? Do you not blush, you stubborn one, at these words?

What is this, 'To surrender oneself to God'? It is so that what He wills, he also wills; and what He does not will, he also does not. How then will this happen? How could it happen otherwise, except by considering the will and governance of God? What has He given me as my own and under my control? What has He reserved for Himself? He has given me a free will: and He willed that those things which are in my power could neither be hindered nor prohibited. But how could He make a body of clay <note>original: "corpus luteum." Therefore, He subjected possessions, vessels, and houses to the rotation of the universe..."

<margin>Seneca, On Tranquility of Mind, chapter 14.</margin>
The soul that desires to become its own master must certainly be called back from all external things into itself: let it withdraw, as much as possible, from the affairs of others, and apply itself to itself; let it not feel its losses, and let it interpret even adversities kindly. This is where the soul begins to be its own; this is the liberty of the soul.

<margin>Augustine, The City of God, book 4, chapter 3.</margin>
Augustine says no differently: "The good man," he says, "even if he serves as a slave, is free; the evil man, even if he reigns as a king, is a slave—to as many masters as he has vices."

<margin>Francis Schott in the *Life of Borgia*, book 1, chapter 12.</margin>**Francis Borgia**, Duke of Gandia, lived eighteen years in wonderful harmony with his wife **Leonora**. When she fell ill, seeing that he was about to be robbed of his other half, he prayed more frequently, enlisting the prayers of pious people, as well as alms and fasting. Sometimes entering his private room alone, with all witnesses removed, he earnestly pleaded with God with many tears, wishing his wife to be safe and surviving. When, behold, he seemed to hear clearly an inner voice (as he later recounted) which said: *“If you wish your wife to live longer, let it be according to your judgment; but it is not expedient for you.”* Disturbed by this, he did not doubt—he did not doubt in the least—that it was the voice of God; for he was silently reproached for not knowing what he was asking for. Thus, dissolved in tears again, he burst forth with these words from the depths of his heart: *“Lord God, why is this granted to me, that you should commit to my judgment what is in your power alone? It is of great importance to me to follow your will in all things. For who knows better what is for my benefit than you, my God?”*

### VI.

Thus, in all the most difficult circumstances, our will must be conformed to the divine. And behold, another far more illustrious example of this conformation. King David, the son of Jesse, joined his own will to the divine with such a tight bond of agreement that God, as if congratulating Himself regarding this man, said: <margin>Acts 13:22</margin> *I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will perform all my wills.* <note>The original Latin uses the plural *voluntates* (wills) to emphasize David's readiness to follow every specific command or desire of God.</note> "I have found," He says, as if He had searched anxiously and waited a long time until He found him. This eulogy granted by God to the king of Hebron <note>Hebron was the city where David was first anointed king over Judah.</note> exceeds all titles of honor.

Christ, who was in every way most obedient to the Father, encouraged us by His own example in this matter: <margin>John 6:38 and 4:34</margin> *Because I have come down,* He says, *from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.* And: *My food is to do the will of him who sent me, so that I may complete his work.* For this is the reason I have come down from heaven. ...[fearlessly, not for the sake of] goods, as Satan slandered Job <note>The adversary Satan argued that Job only served God because of his material wealth and protection</note>; nor out of fear of punishment, lest I be cast into hell, but with a single eye <note>A biblical metaphor for having a pure, focused intention toward God</note> I look upon your will alone: I will it, because you will it, my God.

Second. **Lovingly**: *Thy will be done* <note>original: "Fiat voluntas tua"</note>; here I look to this alone, that what I do may please you, and that in this way the majesty of your name may be spread through me, your most useless servant <note>A humble reference to Luke 17:10: "We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty"</note>. Third. **Promptly**: *Thy will be done*. To will slowly is the mark of one who is unwilling. The most pleasing acts of obedience are those that are ready and occur easily, where there is no delay. It is characteristic of one who acts willingly to act quickly. As much grace is taken away from a good will as delay is added to it. Therefore, *my heart is ready* <margin>Psalm 107, verse 1</margin>, O God, my heart is ready to do your whole will.

Fourth. **Cheerfully**: Some things we do quickly enough, but not willingly enough. *Not out of sadness or necessity* <margin>2 Corinthians, chapter 9, verse 7</margin>: for *God loves a cheerful giver*. He who sets God's will as his ultimate goal, if any boredom or sorrow intervenes, he swallows it without complaint, for he hungers for those delights, so that he may say: *My food is to do the will of him who sent me* <note>A quote from Jesus in John 4:34</note>. Therefore, *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven*.

Fifth. **Completely.** <note>original: "Integre"</note> Let *Thy will be done*, without omitting even a "tittle" <note>An "apex" or tittle refers to the smallest stroke or decorative mark in handwriting, signifying that not even the tiniest detail should be ignored</note> that points to it. ...the divine will <note>original: "tate divina," completing the word "voluntate" from the previous page</note>, and we too in our prayers can imitate it in this way: Let the intellect, like a most attentive spectator, contemplate God’s Power, Eternity, Wisdom, Beauty, and His infinite and immense Blessedness. But let the will rejoice that God is the infinite good, the fountain of all riches, needing nothing, able to do all things, generous toward all, and present in all things. Theologians <note>A reference to Scholastic authors who defined the "act of love" as taking joy in the beloved's excellence.</note> consider this to be the greatest and most perfect act of divine love. For just as no love can be greater than that with which God loves Himself, so also our love cannot be better than if it becomes daily more conformed to that divine love. It is a maxim of the philosophers <note>A classic Aristotelian definition: "To love is to will the good of another."</note> that *to love* is nothing other than to wish good to someone. This being established, it follows that the more good we wish for someone, the more we love them. But we cannot wish for a more immense good for God than that which He is Himself—the most immense good of all goods. Therefore, we cannot love God more ardently than by wishing Him all His own goods. On this account, in this way especially, the will of God shall be done on earth as it is in heaven.

### BOOK II.

...you have submitted yourself deeply to the [divine] will, and in that which it determines concerning you, you acquiesce without any complaint. To this point, that saying of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> applies most remarkably; while examining the command given to the **First Parents** <note>original: "Protoplastis," a term for Adam and Eve as the first-formed humans.</note> about not touching the apple, he assumed the persona of Adam and said: "If the tree is good," he says, "why do I not touch it? If it is evil, what is it doing in paradise?" To him, God replies: "It is in paradise for this reason: because it is good; but I do not want you to touch it, because I want you as an obedient servant, not one who talks back." Why is this? Because you are the servant, and I am the Lord. Behold, there are a thousand reasons contained under this one: because God is our Lord, and He has set forth His will for us to follow, not to judge; and since we are servants, it is most just that we go this way, wherever the will of the Lord leads us.

<margin>Genesis chapter 3, verse 1.</margin>
The **Apostate Angel** <note>The fallen angel, Satan, in the form of the serpent.</note> most cunningly and wickedly asked in paradise: "Why did God command you?" The question should have been: "Why do you not eat the fruit of this tree?" For to this question, the most fitting response would have been: "Because God commanded it." But that most subtle serpent snatched away the answer and made a question out of it: "Why did God command?" Therefore, whenever it is known that God wills something, it is no longer permitted to ask: "Why this?" The most compelling cause of all causes is: ***God so wills it.*** When **Abraham** was commanded to sacrifice his son, what reasons could he not have devised and argued in opposition? Yet he remained silent and obeyed; this one thing was enough for him: ***God so wills it.***

V. Parents, by way of testing the natural disposition <note>original: "genio"</note> of their children, often ask: "Would it not be pleasing on such a fine day to retire to the garden, or go to the countryside? What if today we give our books a holiday <note>original: "missionem demus," literally to give a discharge or release</note>, and substitute playing cards <note>original: "chartulas pictas," literally "little painted papers," a common term for cards</note> in their place?" If the children respond, **"Just as it please my lord father; as my lord father wishes, etc.,"** they provide proof of the best upbringing and a mature wisdom. 

But if they do not hide how greedy they are for little walks and play, and even before their parents have given the nod, they already fly out into the sunshine, they display a specimen of a character that is not good. Then the Father says best: "Hey boy, put away the playthings; today you must go to your lessons." Here we see the downcast face, the sadness in the eyes, the muttering, and not the reading of books, but an idle flipping of pages; here is often weeping and complaints against the "tyranny" of the parents. 

Behold these foolish children, who are so little manageable at their parents' whim. We are very often just like them; most prone toward every little delight and easily muttering when God, the best of fathers, either disturbs our play or sends us away to work. If we are wise, we will emulate the best-instructed children, and we will never say anything other than this: **"As it pleases the Lord Father."** We are prompt and ready to go or not to go; to do or not to do; to work or to suffer, whatever the Father has willed.

### CHAPTER V.

->*What the signs and indicators are of a human will conformed to the divine.*<-

The Romans placed no value on a soldier who did not have strong ribs and muscular arms <note>original: "torosos lacertos," referring to brawny or bulging muscles</note> to carry any burden whatsoever; furthermore, his weapons had to be polished and shining, and he had to have the greatest confidence in his Emperor. Let no one boast that he is a soldier of Christ, nor believe himself a devotee of the divine will, unless he discovers certain signs in himself that his own will depends upon the divine will in all things. In this matter, so that one might test oneself, he should observe these signs or indicators.

**I. Sign.** To desire to do all things at the command of the divine will, and therefore to begin no business without first imploring divine help. He who follows God's will undertakes no task without first asking God to be his helper. If anything seems of greater importance, or more difficult to do, he demands help from God more frequently. Let this be like a law for those who handle serious business and "sit at the helm" <note>The "helm" (original: "clavum") refers to those in positions of leadership or steering the "ship of state" or a household</note>, never to undertake anything rashly without consulting the Lord. **III. Sign. The greatest possible distrust of oneself.** This is a truly Christian virtue, scarcely known to the ancient idolaters <note>original: "idololatris"; a common term in early modern theological texts referring to the pagan philosophers of Greece and Rome who, despite their wisdom, were seen as lacking Christian humility</note>. He who distrusts himself does not attribute even the most happy successes to his own strength or his own industry, but ascribes them entirely to divine power and goodness; he imputes errors and whatever stems from them to himself, and most faithfully observes the warning of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose writings emphasize the necessity of divine grace over human effort</note>: *Let your entire confidence* <note>original: "praesumptio"; here meaning reliance or self-assurance</note> *be in God, so that you recognize that without God you can do nothing at all, and in God, you can do all things.* Nonetheless, such a person, though they distrust and despair of all their own affairs, does not neglect to do what lies within their power; they lean on God with a confidence all the more certain because they have none in themselves. They know they can do nothing, and yet can do everything—but only with God. They work indeed according to their strength, but they expect the entire outcome of their labor from the divine will, bearing with an even mind all those things which are not evil, except to the one who bears them poorly.

How differently behave those who trust in themselves, their own strength, and their own skill; who trust in the counsels of their own prudence! How eloquent they are in the praise of their own affairs, how generously they laud themselves, while in the meantime acting slackly in many things, excessive in their self-confidence?

A military commander <term>Dux militiæ; literally a leader of the army</term> who has undertaken the defense of a fortress will, while the enemy is still far off, consider the weaker and unprotected parts of the site, provide for the supply of food, arrange the engines of war, and prepare himself against every possible attack; for he knows that the enemy is not to be trusted. ...because I see that this is of your will: Your will, my God, has imposed this silence upon me.

<margin>Boethius, Book 4 of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, prose 6.</margin>
Severinus Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose work was a staple of medieval and Renaissance education</note>, a man most illustrious in both his writings and his life, puts it quite remarkably: "Who else," he asks, "is either the preserver of good things or the driver-away of evil things, but God, the ruler and director of minds? When He looks out from the high watchtower of His providence, He recognizes what is suitable for each person, and what He knows to be suitable, He provides. Therefore, whatever you see happening here contrary to your hope, it is indeed a right order in the reality of things; though to your own opinion, it seems like a perverse confusion." He who surrenders himself entirely to the divine will trusts not in his own opinion, but in the order of things, which he approves as being for the best by keeping silent.

It sometimes happens that a master of a more impulsive temperament, having entered his servant’s quarters, knocks everything down, disturbs, and mixes everything up, and then quickly leaves so that the author of the deed is not caught in the act. The servant, returning home and seeing all his belongings in disarray, becomes severely enraged; but when he hears that it was done by his master, he falls silent and grows calm. So David says of himself: "I was silent and did not open my mouth." Why so? *Because you did it* <note>original: "Quoniam tu fecisti"</note>. In exactly this way, one who has offered himself entirely to the divine will indeed feels adversity, but consoles himself with divine Providence; he is not ignorant of the fact that he will gain nothing through vain complaints.

<margin>
Psalm 120,
verses 1
and 2.

</margin>

Whatever happens in the world (with the exception of sin), by whomever or however it happens, it must be said to happen by divine will. All things that happen, God wills to happen; whatever God does not will, most certainly does not happen.

<margin>Epictetus, Book 4, *Discourses*, Chapter 7, and the *Enchiridion*, Chapter 13. <note>Epictetus (c. 50–135 AD) was a Stoic philosopher who taught that while we cannot control external events, we can control our reaction to them.</note></margin>
Hence, Epictetus wisely said: "I always prefer that which happens." And to persuade everyone of this same thing, he said: "Do not demand that things happen as you wish. We confirm this from the secrets of Theology: Theologians define this matter with these words: "God wills every created good existing in actuality; but whatever happens outside of sin is a created good existing in actuality; therefore, whatever happens in the world, God wills it to happen, provided sin is absent."
