The Pontiff often visited his painter, and he was not unaware of the man's artful boldness; although he by no means approved of it, he feigned not to see it for a certain reason, thinking to himself: "As long as he finishes the work, he will soon feel the errors of his brush in prison, dining on only bread and water."

Certainly, this Pontiff wanted the tribunal of the Supreme Judge to be painted, and this for the benefit of the viewers, not for the contempt or injury of anyone; yet, for certain ends, he knowingly and willingly did not prevent it. In the same way, God wants us to "paint" for eternity and produce immortal works; but as we wander astray in our feelings and our hand, we place now these people, now those in **the Underworld** <note>original: "Orcus", a classical term for the realm of the dead, here used for Hell</note>—that is, we are unjustly harmful in various ways toward those whom we consider our enemies. But we also commit many other faults while performing our work. Nevertheless, the "painting" of the most diverse things in the world is being worked out. For there is a marvelous connection, sequence, and harmony of all things, such that individual parts which might seem deformed or certainly less beautiful on their own, are far more beautiful when joined to the rest. God, however, is most patient with delay...

<margin>Wisdom chapter 6, verse 8.</margin>

### A brief explanation of the following image.

<margin>Acts ch. 13 v. 22</margin>
King David was the most perfect model of a person conformed to the divine will. A witness truly beyond all objection is God Himself, who said: *I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will carry out all my desires.* <note>original: *voluntates meas* (literally "my wills"). The plural suggests total obedience to every specific command or desire of God.</note>

The **Sunflower** <note>original: *Heliotropium*. In 17th-century devotional literature, the sunflower was a common symbol for the soul because it turns its "face" to follow the sun (representing God) throughout the day.</note>, blooming with smaller flowers similar to itself, represents the great growth in virtue that comes from this single conformity to God’s will—a quality I would rightly call the mother of all virtues.

**Two hearts**, that of God and that of man, are joined in such an embrace that they appear to be a single heart. The words written within the divine heart are: **RECEIVE, GIVE BACK, FLEE**. That is: *Receive the blessing, Give back thanks, and Flee whatever is contrary to the divine will.* The human heart rightly responds: **WHAT GOD WILLS**, that is precisely what I also will. From this union, a most beautiful garland from paradise encircles both hearts. Here, the sword of sorrow and grief is cast away; here, the crown of roses woven from fleeting pleasure falls aside. A **winged messenger** <note>original: *Aliger*. A poetic term for an angel.</note> from heaven brings the most joyful news of eternal happiness, by which a person devoted to the divine will is invited to immortality. No one can be miserable when called by such a blessed messenger.

### CHAPTER I.

*How much tranquility of mind the Conforming of the human will to the divine brings.*

We have already discussed the means by which we may know the divine will and how we might join our own to it. Now, we must proceed to discuss what benefit arises if the human will is always most closely joined to the divine.

I. God is so generous with His riches and gifts that He has not only determined to bless us with eternal delights, but—as if anticipating the day of eternity to make us more ready and eager for all things—He sends from His table a first taste <note>original: *promulsidem* — a Roman term for an appetizer or first course meant to whet the appetite</note> of the heavenly banquet, and commands us to sample at least a small taste of eternal happiness. Thus, even in this foul hospital <note>original: *nosocomio* — a place for the sick, used here as a metaphor for the suffering inherent in mortal life</note> of mortality, there is no lack of what we might call a preliminary course to that great and eternal supper. Even in this lower world, there is some measure of rest; here, too, are comforts sent from heaven. Nor is this achieved at great expense; there is need only for a will conformed to the divine.

# ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

...tranquillity: for here there is no need to strive with unusual severity of life, nor with frequent fasts, nor with lengthy vigils; a single noble **WILL** <note>original: *VELLE* — the infinitive "to will" used as a noun, representing the core faculty of human choice.</note> accomplishes this whole business. But this **WILL** must be renewed daily and firmly established: to never knowingly and prudently admit anything contrary to the divine will. For thus, says 

<margin>Chrysostom, sermon on Zacchaeus, near the end of the second part.</margin>

Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his eloquence.</note>, *willing brings about the ability to do, just as not willing brings about the inability*. Great is the power of the will, which makes us able to do what we wish, and unable to do those things we do not wish.

But if someone should commit himself to God in the morning in this way: "O my Lord and my God, I offer myself to you for your every good pleasure <note>original: *beneplacitum* — God's gracious will or what is pleasing to Him.</note>; today, knowingly and intentionally, I shall do nothing against your will"; yet on this same day he enters a forbidden tavern <note>original: *ganeam* — a place of gluttony or low-class eating house.</note> or an infamous brothel, or rashly indulges himself in other opportunities for vice, this man must be judged to be playing games with God, and to be offering bread with one hand, but a scorpion with the other. To promise oneself to be utterly subject to the divine will, yet nevertheless to lay snares for the wealth or the reputation and name of others, to willingly admit envy into oneself, not to be overtaken by anger but to summon it of one's own accord—this is to joke with God; it is to push forward the arrival of vices and to open the door to those who have scarcely even asked to be let in. And what kind of sign of love is this? "I love you, but take this blow from me"; or: "I will not allow myself to be separated from you, but when the opportunity... <note>The sentence continues on the next page with the word "opportunity" (occasio).</note>

<summary>This page argues that spiritual peace is achieved not through ascetic hardship, but through a sincere and daily renewal of the will to follow God. It warns against the hypocrisy of professing submission to God while knowingly indulging in vice or harming others.</summary>

<sig>K 5</sig>

...opportunity <note>original: *occasio* — continuing from the previous page.</note> invites him onto the narrow path of a cliff, those things which I had previously soothed with words, I now cast down into the abyss with my hand. To these, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, as cited on the previous page.</note> responds: *For no one*, he says, *can be excused as if they wished and yet were unable; since it is clear that they were unable for the reason that they did not wish to be, so that the one who is unwilling might be condemned by the example of the one who is willing, and the one who is willing might be rewarded because he fulfilled what he desired.*

<margin>Chrysostom, sermon on Zacchaeus.</margin>

IV. Therefore, that conversation between the two religious men is not difficult to grasp, and we are forced to admit that the path is blocked to no one toward that peak of Tranquility; the door to this paradise is closed to no one: whoever can do this one thing, ***to Will what God wills*** <note>original: *Velle quod vult Deus*</note>, has already entered; no people of any rank, sex, or age are barred from here. Truly, there are two principal points in the recorded conversation of such excellent instruction, that to have understood them well is to have won the prize here.

First: To drink deeply into the soul that whatever happens occurs through divine providence, which disposes all things toward its own end and toward happiness, as has pleased the most secret judgment of God from all eternity. All things run their course according to a certain and eternally spoken law. Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Roman Stoic philosopher whose views on fate often appealed to Christian writers.</note> speaks beautifully of this: *Cause hangs upon cause*, he says, *and a long order of things draws along both private and public affairs. Therefore, everything must be endured bravely: because all things do not happen by chance, as we suppose, but they arrive by design.* <note>original: *veniunt* — literally "they come," implying they follow a pre-ordained path rather than "falling" (*incidunt*) by accident.</note> Long ago...

<margin>Seneca, *On Providence*, chapter 5.</margin>

# ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

...se <note>original: *con-stitutum* — completing the thought from the previous page: "All things run their course as it has been determined."</note> as it has been determined: what you should rejoice in, and what you should weep for; and although the life of individuals seems to be distinguished by great variety, the sum of it all comes to one point. We, who are destined to perish, have received things that will perish. Why do we feel such indignation? Why do we complain? We were prepared for this. Let nature use her own bodies as she wishes; let us, joyful and strong in all circumstances, reflect that nothing of our own is being lost.

The second point: To do what lies within one's power, and to entrust all other matters to divine Providence with the most generous confidence; to live content with one's own lot, not to pry into another's, nor to envy anyone a more blessed state. These are the things that lead into the impregnable fortress of Tranquility <note>original: *Tranquillitas* — a state of inner peace and spiritual stability</note>; this is that full armor <note>original: *panoplia* — a complete set of armor, referencing the spiritual "whole armor of God."</note> of all virtues. Truly, those who love these fleeting things never put on this armor—those who treat these things as if they were their own and lasting goods, who wish to be admired because of them, and who do not sufficiently trust in divine Providence. These people collapse at the motion of the slightest injuries; they lie prostrate and mourn when false and fickle amusements abandon their vain and childish souls, which are ignorant of any solid pleasure. But he who does not puff himself up in prosperous times, nor shrink when things change, trusts most fully in divine Providence regarding himself; he maintains an unconquered spirit of proven firmness against either condition. He is fortified by the full armor of all virtues. In a word: **He wills what God wills.**

### BOOK III.

### CHAPTER II.

*Whether it is possible for someone never to be saddened, and whether this can be achieved through that art by which we conform our will to the divine will.*

<margin>Proverbs chapter 12, verse 21.</margin>
Solomon, that ocean of human wisdom and great marvel, declared most freely: *Whatever happens to the righteous man shall not make him sad.* <note>original: *Non contristabit justum quicquid ei acciderit.*</note> The most wise King is speaking here of accidental things—those things that happen to a good mind contrary to what it desires. It is as if he were saying: Voluntary evils, such as sins and wrongdoings, certainly keep a good man anxious and cause him pain; but those mockeries of fortune—the loss of resources, the loss of honor, the toll on one's health, the funerals of loved ones—do not afflict or distress the righteous man. In fact, he very often counts these things as benefits; he does not think of them as evils, but believes them to be an exercise of patience, and gives thanks to God for them, as is only right. For to a good mind, every calamity is an opportunity for virtue.

Therefore, Hugo <note>likely Hugh of Saint Victor (c. 1096–1141), a prominent mystical theologian</note>, weighing that phrase "whatever happens to him" with great insight, says: "Just as an 'accident' is defined by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle; medieval authors frequently referred to him simply as 'The Philosopher'</note> as something that can be present or absent without the destruction of the subject; so too, present tribulation and hardship may be present or absent without causing sadness or disturbance to the righteous man."

Furthermore, the Apostle Paul is a most abundant witness to the fact that the righteous man receives any external evils with an upright and cheerful mind, saying: *I am filled...* <note>The text likely continues with 2 Corinthians 7:4: "I am filled with comfort, I am exceeding joyful in all our tribulation."</note>

<summary>This page explores the Stoic and Christian idea that a righteous person can remain untroubled by external misfortunes (like loss of wealth or health) by viewing them as opportunities for virtue rather than true evils. It cites Solomon, Aristotle, and Hugh of Saint Victor to argue that while sin causes true sorrow, external hardships do not disturb the inner peace of one aligned with God's will.</summary>

On the contrary, just as if you were to cast a tiny spark into the vast sea, you would extinguish it immediately; in the same way, any distress, however great, if it falls upon a mind with a clear conscience, immediately perishes and vanishes. This same "Golden-Mouthed" teacher, in order to place the matter more clearly before one's eyes, compared the mind to the heavens. "The sky," he says, "is higher than the storms and the rains. Indeed, when the sky is covered with clouds, it is thought to suffer, but it suffers nothing. So also we, even if we are thought to suffer, we suffer nothing—that is, sorrow, like a cloud, [ob-]..."

...mind, we are thought to be overshadowed, but we are not saddened. "What pain does the virtue of the mind not hide? For I would not deny that the sea is deep just because the shores are shallow; nor that the sky is bright because it is occasionally covered with clouds; nor that the earth is fertile because in some places there is barren gravel; nor that the crops are joyful because they are accustomed to have sterile oats mixed in. In the same way, consider the harvest of a blessed conscience <note>original: "beatę messem conscientiæ" — The author uses the metaphor of a harvest to describe the internal rewards of a good life.</note> to be interrupted by some sharp pain; nevertheless, if anything of adversity or bitterness happens to occur, it is hidden by the sheaves of a blessed life, just as sterile oats are hidden, or as the bitterness of darnel <note>A type of weed often found among wheat, historically considered bitter or even toxic.</note> is covered by the sweetness of the grain." Therefore, whatever happens to the righteous man shall not make him sad. He will feel the sadness, but he will not give his consent to it; the sky will be covered with clouds, but it will not be overturned; the darnel will mix itself with the wheat, but it will not do harm. To not feel one's misfortunes is not the mark of a human; but not to endure them is not the mark of a man. <note>original: "Non sentire mala sua, nō est hominis; at non ferre, non est viri." — A stoic-leaning sentiment: feeling pain is natural, but being broken by it is a failure of character.</note>

I. Nor is it only Christian wisdom that grasps this: this strength of mind was not unknown even to the ancients. The poet of Venusia <note>A reference to Horace (65–8 BC), who was born in Venusia. He is one of the most famous Roman lyric poets.</note> truly sang:
<margin>Horace, Book 3 of *Odes*, Ode 3.</margin>
> *The man who is just and firm in his purpose,*
> *Neither the heat of citizens ordering wrongs,*
> *Nor the face of a threatening tyrant*
> *Shakes his solid mind: —*
> *If the world were to break and fall,*
> *The ruins would strike him unafraid.*

The second piece of advice: A plaster must be applied to the injured part, not to the healthy one, nor to one where it does not fit. Eye-salve <term>collyrium: a liquid or semi-solid medicinal preparation for the eyes</term> heals the eyes, not the arms; a pill <term>catapotium: a medicinal bolus or pill meant to be swallowed</term> is to be taken for the stomach, not used for binding the foot; a poultice <term>malagma: a soft, soothing medicinal mass or plaster applied to the skin</term> should be applied to the sore, not to a neighboring part. In exactly the same way, Sadness heals neither financial loss, nor loss of honor, nor disease, nor any of these evils. Consume yourself with grief, fill everything with tears, and you will gain not a bit; you will not recover money, honor, or health through mourning, but you will only increase the loss and the pain. The reason for this is as follows: Sadness is the proper remedy for sin; this plague is cured by this antidote; apply this poultice to this sore. Grieve for having sinned, not for having lost money. 
<margin>Chrysostom, Homily 5 to the People.</margin>
Chrysostom, most skillfully reminding us of this, says: "Someone has been fined; he was saddened, but he did not reverse the fine. Someone lost a son; he grieved, but he did not raise the dead. Someone was flogged; he grieved, but he did not undo the insult. Someone fell into illness..."

...even if you do not know it. <note>This completes the thought from the previous page regarding God's providence.</note> But this very thing which He redeemed—your soul—offer this to Him. And if you ask me, "How shall I offer my soul to Him, since He already holds it in His power?" I will answer: through holy character, chaste thoughts, and fruitful deeds. <margin>Psalm 54, verse 6. <note>The text cites Psalm 53, but in modern numbering, this is typically Psalm 54:6.</note></margin> 
"I will sacrifice to you," he says, "voluntarily." <note>original: "Voluntarie sacrificabo tibi."</note>

This very concept is wonderfully pleasing to any of us: when someone devotes themselves to us with such a generous offering. Once, when many people were offering many things to Socrates <note>The famous Greek philosopher (c. 470–399 BCE).</note> according to their individual means, Aeschines, a poor student, said: "I find nothing worthy of you that I am able to give; in this one way, I feel my poverty. Therefore, I give you the only thing I have: myself. I ask that you look kindly upon this gift, such as it is, and consider that while others gave you much, they kept more for themselves." To which Socrates replied: "Why should you not have given me a great gift—unless perhaps you value yourself at a low price? I shall take care, therefore, to return you to yourself better than I received you." By this gift, Aeschines' spirit surpassed the wealth of Alcibiades <note>A prominent and extremely wealthy Athenian statesman.</note> and all the generosity of the rich young men.
<margin>Seneca, book 1 on *Benefits*, chapter 8. <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher.</note></margin>

And this must be done every single day, not just once or twice, but more often, even a hundred or a thousand times, especially when one feels oneself changing or under attack, or when one notices something failing to succeed or, conversely, succeeding happily. In those moments, one must cry out: **"O my Lord and my God, I offer myself to you for all your good pleasure; your will be done."** <note>original: "O Dominus meus, & Deus meus, ego me tibi offero in omne beneplacitum tuum: fiat voluntas tua."</note> This practice brings patience in adversity and sobriety and moderation in prosperity. ### CHAPTER IV.

*That the entire perfection of man consists in the Alignment of the human will with the divine will.*

All human actions derive their worth from the goal they seek; thus, they are as good or as bad as that goal happens to be. Truly, however, we shall find no goal for our actions that is better or more sublime than the divine will—that is, God Himself. Therefore, no actions are better or more sublime than those which are closest to this goal. 

This is the source of that famous saying by <term>Basil the Great</term> <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian (Basil of Caesarea) known for his influential monastic rules.</note>, that the entire sum of holiness for a Christian lies in this: that he attributes the causes of all things, whether great or small, to the one and only God, and most readily submits himself to the divine will in everything. This is what the holy Fathers and teachers of the spiritual life so often and so strongly recommend as *Resignation* <note>original: "Resignatio." In this theological context, it refers to the intentional surrender of one’s own desires and self-interest to God's providence.</note>. It is the foundation of all inner peace, as it places a person in the safest possible hand—the hand of God. It works in such a way that the person no longer wishes to belong to themselves, but to God; they no longer live for themselves, but for God, and they do nothing except for God’s sake, remaining just as content in hard times as in prosperous ones. **THE GOOD.** Chrysostom says most excellently: "That which is done according to the will of God," he says, "although it may seem to be wicked, is nevertheless altogether pleasing and acceptable to God. Conversely, that which is done outside the will of God, and differently than He wishes it to be done, although it is thought acceptable to God, is nevertheless the worst and most unjust of all things." <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching; here, he argues that divine command overrides human perceptions of morality.</note>

The annals of the Kings provide a proof of this matter. A prophet was about to rebuke King Ahab by divine command because he had spared the King of Syria, whom he had captured in war, against the will of God. <note>King Ahab of Israel had spared Ben-Hadad of Syria, a decision that the biblical narrative presents as a failure to execute God's judgment.</note> However, so that he might not be recognized as a rebuker at first glance, he approached a com-

<margin>1 Kings, chapter 20, verse 36.</margin>
panion: *By the word of the Lord,* he said, *strike me.* <note>original: "In fermone Domini... percute me"</note> The man was unwilling; for he held it as a point of religious scruple to wound a prophet. But soon he heard a terrifying decree: *You shall depart from me,* said the seer, *and a lion shall strike you.* It happened as he predicted. Therefore, approaching another man, the prophet said: *Strike me.* That man struck the prophet and wounded him. Not only did he do this with impunity, but he earned praise for it. "What could be more absurd than this?" asks Chrysostom. He who struck the prophet escaped unharmed; he who spared him paid the penalty. Such is the importance of following or rejecting the rule of the divine will. Once the divine will is known to anyone, it is a sin for him to ask further: "Why is it so?" In place of all causes is the fact that God wills it so.

Therefore, the safest summit of **Christian perfection** is to surrender oneself as fully as possible to the divine will, and to cease being one's own, so that one may become God's.

I. The son of Themistocles <note>Themistocles (c. 524–459 BC) was a famous Athenian statesman and general. This anecdote was a popular rhetorical tool used to illustrate the power of influence.</note> once boasted that the entire Athenian Republic was governed by him, for all the citizens wanted whatever he himself wanted. When people wondered at the young man's incredibly bold claim, he explained: "Whatever I want, my mother also wants (for she loves her son most tenderly); but whatever my mother wants, my father Themistocles also wants; and whatever pleases my father, it is already well-established that it immediately pleases Athens. Therefore," he said, "the Athenian Republic is shaped according to my command." 

In exactly the same way—and with far better right—a person of most upright will might say: "Whatever I want, the entire heavenly host wants." For what I want, God wants (since I never want anything except what God wants); and whatever God wants, all the ranks of the Blessed and the entire orders of Angels want. ### BOOK III.

N 2

...then he exalts their honor so far as to make them the very kinsmen of Christ! Truly, the highest good of life is the union of the human will with the divine.

A holy man <note>Likely referring to a specific spiritual father or theologian, such as Tauler or Thomas à Kempis, common in such devotional literature.</note> used to say: **Whatever you will, that you are.** Indeed, our will, when joined to the divine, is of such great power that whatever we seriously and with our whole intention desire to be, that we are. No one ardently desires to be humble, patient, modest, or even generous, who does not become the very person they desire to be. *Whatever you will, that you are.* That same man adds: If you cannot perform or bestow great things, at least maintain a great will, and extend it toward the infinite. Are you poor? You can nevertheless be of such a mind that, if riches were available, you would distribute them most generously to the needy. Are you of little strength? You can nevertheless offer yourself in such a way that if you had a thousand souls and a thousand heads, you would not refuse to sacrifice those thousand souls, heads, and lives for Christ. Are you afflicted, and do you seem miserable to yourself? Join your will to the divine, and you will be most happy. He is truly miserable who cannot rule himself; he whom vices quarrel over—just as cities quarrel over Homer <note>original: "de Homero civitates litigant"; a reference to the seven cities that claimed to be the birthplace of the poet Homer. They interpret all adversity as a trial of themselves, and they trace everything back to the divine will. Therefore, they do not shrink from hard and difficult things, nor do they complain about God or divine permissions <note>The theological concept of "permissive will," where God allows certain hardships to occur for a greater purpose.</note>. Whatever happens, they take it in good part, they turn it toward the good, and they attribute everything to the divine will and Providence.

They say that Mount Olympus in Macedonia is of such wonderful height that neither winds, nor rains, nor snows ever reach its summit:

### A brief explanation of the following image.

When the human will is resistant <note>original: *refractaria*; stubborn or unyielding.</note> toward the divine, it acts much like King Pharaoh, who, in his extreme defiance toward God, proved clearly by the ruin of himself and his people what it means TO NOT WILL <note>original: *NOLLE*</note> what God wills. The divine heart indeed constantly invites: FOLLOW [ME] <note>original: *SEQVERE*</note>. But the pride of the human heart, which the peacock's feathers represent, responds with that Laconian <note>original: *Laconis*; referring to a characteristically brief and blunt Spartan-like refusal.</note> reply: I WILL NOT SERVE <note>original: *NON SERVIAM*; a phrase traditionally attributed to the rebellion of Lucifer.</note>. Through such defiance, it breaks whatever chains are placed upon it. 

The devil drags such a will wherever he wishes with those most powerful snares of pride, greed, and lust. But no one resists the divine will with impunity. Punishments are prepared for the rebellious. When other penalties cease, even the sea acts as an executioner <note>A reference to the Exodus story where Pharaoh’s army was drowned in the Red Sea.</note>. 

This same separation of the human will from the divine is represented by a covered Sun and a broken Sunflower <term>Heliotropium: literally "sun-turner," a plant that naturally turns its face toward the sun; here used as a symbol of the soul that ought to follow God.</term>. Here it must be observed: just as God loves those who love Him, so He abandons those who abandon Him, and at last cries out: *I have called and you refused; I also will laugh at your destruction.* <margin>Proverbs 1:24, 26</margin> Therefore, either will what God wills, or perish.

### ON THE OBSTACLES
### TO CONFORMING THE HUMAN WILL
# TO THE DIVINE.

### CHAPTER I.

*Those things which most greatly hinder the conformity of the human will with the divine.*

If the keys to a house or a city are entrusted to someone, the power to enter that house or city at will is granted along with them. Christ the Lord sometimes seeks the keys to the inner chambers of the heart for a long time until He obtains them and gains free access to the heart. We show so little courtly courtesy <note>original: "aulicæ humanitatis" — referring to the refined manners expected in a royal court</note> to the most generous guest of all. Louis Blosius <note>a famous 16th-century Benedictine mystic and spiritual writer</note> tells a story most worthy of being known regarding the blessed virgin Gertrude <note>Saint Gertrude the Great (1256–1302), a German Benedictine mystic</note>.

<margin>
*Blosius, Book 4 of "The Insinuations of Divine Piety," Chapter 23.*
</margin>

Christ, appearing visibly to her, said: "In this hand I carry health, and in this one, disease: choose, daughter, whichever pleases you." What should Gertrude do here? Should she choose health? It would seem like impudence. Should she prefer disease over health? It would be attributed to excessive modesty. Certainly, it is human custom that when a one friend offers such a choice to another, the latter should choose the less valuable thing to demonstrate modesty; thus, Gertrude ought to have chosen disease, perhaps to avoid the torments of the next world <note>referring to the belief that suffering in this life reduces purification needed in the afterlife</note>.

<summary>This page introduces Book Four, focusing on what prevents humans from aligning their will with God's. It uses the metaphor of "keys to the heart" and recounts a vision of Saint Gertrude the Great being asked to choose between health and sickness.</summary>

<keywords>free will, Saint Gertrude, Louis Blosius, divine will, spiritual obstacles, sickness and health</keywords>

--- Page 230 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of Saint Gertrude the Great from the previous page. Having been asked by Christ to choose between health and sickness, she now gives her response. The catchword "petra" at the top of the OCR transcription likely refers to the completion of the word "impetra" at the end of the page, a common printer's mark for continuity.</meta>

-> ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL <-

She would not have chosen unwisely had she imitated Catherine of Siena <note>Saint Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), a Dominican mystic who, in a vision, was offered a choice by Jesus between a golden crown and a crown of thorns; she chose the thorns to be more like Christ.</note>, who greatly preferred a crown of thorns to a golden crown. However, Gertrude chose even more prudently and better: she chose neither. Instead, with her hands folded in the shape of a cross over her breast and falling to her knees, she said: "O my Lord, I strive for this with all my prayers—that you look not to my will, but to yours. Therefore, I am ready for either, and I choose neither. It is yours, my Lord, to discern whether you should leave me with health or with sickness."

To her, Christ replied: "Whoever desires to be visited by me more often," He said, "should offer me the key to their own will, and never ask for it back."

Instructed by this, Gertrude composed a brief prayer <note>original: "precatiunculam" — a diminutive form of 'prayer,' implying a short, focused aspiration or 'arrow prayer'</note> in these most earnest words: *Not my will, but Yours be done, my most loving Jesus.*

And she made it her custom to repeat this very thing three hundred and sixty-five times: *Not my will, but Yours be done, my most loving Jesus.* This little prayer indeed seems preferable to a thousand others. He would do very well who repeats this day and night, and even more ardently when adversity strikes most violently. No one is so busy with affairs or burdened by hardships that they cannot speak these most earnest words ten, twenty, thirty, or even a hundred times every single hour: *Not my will, but Yours be done, my most loving Jesus.*

Truly, it seems like no small effort for anyone to always manage to obtain this act of **WILLING** <note>original: "VELLE" — referring to the internal act of the soul actually desiring or choosing what God wants</note> from themselves.

III. With the mind now prepared for Poverty and Contempt, the third offering of oneself follows: **To any illness whatsoever.** Lamps are made of silver or other metals, so skillfully suspended and equipped with such a structure of joints and pivots <note>original: "vertebrarum" — This refers to a gimbal mechanism, an engineering marvel of the time that allowed a lamp to remain perfectly upright even if its frame was shaken or tilted.</note> that no matter how or in what way they are moved, they are never overturned; they preserve their light and always look toward heaven. <margin>Blosius, *Spiritual Guidance*, chapter 10, near the end.</margin> Louis de Blois <note>Also known as Ludovicus Blosius (1506–1566), a Flemish Benedictine monk whose writings on the interior life were highly influential.</note> relates that a virgin of exceptional holiness, when asked by what exercises she had reached such perfection of life, replied: "I was never so overwhelmed by pains that I did not desire to endure even heavier ones for the love of God, considering myself unworthy of such remarkable gifts." Therefore, turning herself to God with her whole soul, she said:

> *My most loving God, be mindful that You are my Lord and Creator. Behold, I offer myself to Your most just judgment, and I resign myself entirely to Your most pleasing will, ready to endure this infernal torment for as long as it shall please You: use me as You wish in time and eternity.*

Thus, devoting herself to the supreme will, she made wonderful progress in divine friendship.

### ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

IV. Fourth, *even toward death, however it may present itself, let the human will offer itself voluntarily*, and let a person seek neither a swift passing nor a long life in any other way than what is pleasing to God. Therefore, let the lover of the divine will say: I desire neither to live long nor to die quickly, but only to obey you, good Jesus, in either this or that. Nor do I prescribe the kind of death by which I wish to pass away; in whatever way you wish to call me to you, I am ready to follow. Only, my God, I might wish to pray against a sudden death, <note>In the historical context, a "sudden and unprovided death" was feared because it left no time for the final sacraments or a last confession.</note> but even here I do not wish to be stubborn against your will; if you wish me to depart by a sudden death, so be it, provided that I live through your grace; I shall always strive to live in your grace. I know that:

<margin>Wisdom, chapter 4, verse 7.</margin>
The just man, if he be overtaken by death, shall be at rest. <note>original: "in refrigerio" — literally "in refreshment" or "coolness," a common biblical term for the peace and relief of the afterlife.</note> Therefore, I neither turn away from an early death nor demand a mature one; nor do I greatly dread a miserable death or one that the eyes shrink from. It is believable that many fall asleep most peacefully in death and yet are snatched to the depths; while many others depart by a horrible and bitter death and are received into heaven. This judgment is more secret than can be visible to the eyes. Therefore, I will readily accept both a gentle and a harsh kind of dying, just as it shall seem good to the Lord.

<margin>Romans, chapter 14, verses 7 and 8.</margin>
For whether we live, or whether we die, we are the Lord's. For none of us lives for himself, and no one dies for himself.

Martin, the bishop of Tours, <note>Saint Martin of Tours (c. 316–397), a Roman soldier turned bishop, famous for his humility and for cutting his cloak in half to share with a beggar.</note> when he was just about to give up his soul, said: **"Lord, if I am still necessary for your people, I do not refuse the labor—"** <note>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "labo-" (for "laborem"), indicating Martin's willingness to keep working/living if God required it.</note>

### BOOK IV.

...labor, thy will be done. Hence, looking upon the virtue of a man of the Church, he said: "O unspeakable man, neither conquered by labor, nor to be defeated by death, who neither feared to die, nor refused to live!" <note>original: "O virum ineffabilem, nec labore victum, nec morte vincendum, qui nec mori timuit, nec vivere recusavit!" This is a traditional antiphon for St. Martin of Tours, a 4th-century bishop known for his total submission to God's service whether in life or death.</note> Thus it is fitting: we must be warned and strengthened in both cases; so that we neither love life too much, nor hate it too much.

<margin>Curtius, Book 5 of the *Histories*.</margin>
Quintus Curtius says: "It is the mark of brave men to despise death more than to hate life." <note>Curtius was a Roman historian; here he is cited to show that even pagan virtue recognized the balance between cowardice and a reckless desire for death.</note> Often the lazy are driven to a low opinion of themselves by the weariness of labor; but virtue leaves nothing unattempted. Death is the final end of all things, and it is sufficient not to go toward it sluggishly.

Both of these, both **living** and **dying**, are to be embraced according to the decree of the divine will. Does God want us to live? Then let us live, whether in happiness or in misery, provided that we strive toward blessedness. Does He want us to die? Then let us die with a most ready spirit, and as the ancient writer warns, let us at least not go to death sluggishly, for it is that which summons us to immortal life.

But alas, how many die with nothing but complaints? Who departs without refusing, who without groaning? Yet this is not to submit oneself entirely to the divine will, nor to be content with the time one was granted.

<margin>Seneca, Book 5 of *On Benefits*, chapter 17.</margin>
We ought to hold ready those things which were given to us for an uncertain duration, and return them without complaint when we are called upon. It is the mark of the worst debtor to heap insults upon his creditor. Days will always seem few if you count them.

Consider that the highest good is not found in time <note>That is, the "highest good" or ultimate happiness does not consist of worldly things or the length of one's life on earth.</note>: however much there is, accept it with good cheer. That the day of your death be postponed for you profits nothing toward true happiness, since a life does not become more blessed by delay, only longer. How much better it is not to count the years of others, but to kindly value one's own and count them as gain. You ought not to complain about what has been taken away, but to give thanks for what has been granted. Because it therefore pleases the divine will that I should die now, I shall die now; I shall die now, and do so willingly.

V. Fifthly and finally, a person devoted to the divine will should offer themselves to God most ready **for all things whatsoever**, whether they may happen in time or in eternity, and do so without any small exception. An eagle’s chick, if it is of noble character, gazes at the sun with the steadiest eyes <note>This refers to a common medieval and ancient belief that a "true" eagle could look directly into the sun without blinking, often used as a metaphor for the soul contemplating God.</note>; so the human will, if it be good, burns for the divine so intensely that it offers itself spontaneously to all things and excludes nothing. 

Who in this regard was more noble than Paul, who pursued the divine will through drawn swords, through gleaming spears, through flying rocks, through the waves of the Ocean, through various whirlwinds, through the most fierce <note>original: "suavissimas" (most pleasant/sweet). For many of the holy martyrs, it was not so difficult to offer their own blood to tyrants as if it were a thing of little value; amidst their torments, they abounded in divine comforts, and thus they easily despised the punishments and even death itself. ### ON THE CONFORMING OF THE WILL

...servants of self-will <term>self-will: "voluntas propria"; the tendency to follow one's own ego and desires rather than the divine or moral law.</term>. For first, this will withdraws and removes itself from the dominion of Him whom it ought to have served by right as its Author <note>original: "auctorem"; referring to God as the creator and rightful authority over the soul.</note>, while it makes itself its own master. But will it be content with this injury alone? It goes even further, and as much as it is in its power, it also seizes and plunders everything that belongs to God. For what limit does human greed <note>original: "cupiditas"</note> set for itself? Does not the man who acquires a small amount of money through usury try to gain the whole world in the same way, if only the possibility were not lacking, and if the power were available to his will? I say with confidence: the entire world would not be enough for anyone who is in the grip of their own self-will.

But would that it were content even with these earthly things, and did not (horrible to say) rage against the Author Himself! This self-will is a cruel beast, a most evil wild animal, a most rapacious she-wolf, and a most savage lioness. This is the most foul leprosy of the soul, because of which one must be immersed in the Jordan <note>A dual reference to the healing of Naaman the Syrian’s leprosy in the River Jordan (2 Kings 5) and the waters of Christian baptism.</note> and imitate Him who did not come to do His own will. Hence, also during His passion, He said: *“Not my will, but yours be done”* <note>Luke 22:42; the words of Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane.</note>.

*“Let self-will cease, and there will be no Hell.”* Therefore, it is neither a childish nor a vain question to ask: Whether, and how, can Hell <note>original: "gehenna"</note> be extinguished? It can be, entirely. It is not an absurd prayer to ask God to destroy the Underworld <note>original: "Orcum"; a classical Roman name for the realm of the dead, used here synonymously with Hell.</note>. God is ready to do this; He asks for this one thing as the reward for His work: *“Let self-will cease, and there will be no Hell.”* But who could drive every single person to the point where each abdicates his own will, and [renounces] it...

### BOOK IV.

...[unusu]al [movements]? <note>Completing the thought from the previous page regarding the rocks' reaction to the Crucifixion.</note> Should I renounce it? Trebellius Pollio <note>A fictional or pseudonymous author of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> relates that Marius <note>Marcus Aurelius Marius, a blacksmith who became a short-lived emperor of the Gallic Empire in 269 AD.</note> was the seventh tyrant of Rome. He was made Emperor on one day; he ruled on the second; and on the third, he was killed by a common soldier. While this soldier was plunging a dagger into Marius's chest, he added these most bitter words: "This is the sword which you yourself made." For he had come from the workshop of a blacksmith <note>original: "cultrarii officina," literally a cutler's or knife-maker's shop</note> to the imperial crown. He who behaves stubbornly against the divine will is rightly mocked in this way: "This is the sword which you yourself made; you are cutting your own throat with your own sword," that is, **BY YOUR OWN WILL**. 

Because the will is so prone to sin, says Caesarius <note>Likely Caesarius of Heisterbach (c. 1180–1240), a Cistercian monk famous for his "Dialogue on Miracles."</note>, there is a hidden cause: the devil has two henchmen worse than himself by whom the will is driven—the Flesh and the World. The Flesh lusts; the Devil ignites what is lusted after; the World throws itself in the way so that the flames are not extinguished. Many vices arise from the Flesh, the World offers many delights, and the Devil employs innumerable deceits. Thus the matter is easily accomplished, as was once shown to the prophet Jeremiah: *Do you not see what these people do in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough, to make cakes...* <note>Jeremiah 7:17-18. The passage describes families cooperating in idolatry.</note>

Trebellius Pollio <note>A Roman historian of the 4th century, one of the purported authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> relates that Marius was the seventh tyrant of Rome. He was made Emperor on one day; he ruled on the second; and on the third he was killed by a common soldier. While the soldier plunged a dagger into the chest of Marius, he added this most bitter remark: "This is the sword which you yourself made." For he had come from the workshop of a cutler <term>cutler (cultrarius)<gloss>a craftsman who makes or repairs knives and blades</gloss></term> to the imperial crown <term>diadem (diadema)<gloss>the headband or crown worn by Roman emperors as a symbol of sovereignty</gloss></term>. 

To him who behaves stubbornly against the divine will, it is justly insulted in this way: "This is the sword which you yourself made." You strike yourself down with your own sword—that is, with your **OWN WILL**. Indeed, the reason why the will is so prone to sinning, says Caesarius <note>Likely referring to Caesarius of Arles or the medieval writer Caesarius of Heisterbach, who used anecdotes to teach moral lessons.</note>, is this: the devil has two henchmen more wicked than himself by whom the will is driven—the Flesh and the World. The Flesh desires; the Devil ignites those desires; the World places itself in the way so that the flames are not extinguished. Many vices arise from the Flesh, the World offers many delights, and the Devil employs innumerable tricks. Thus, the matter is as ready as it was once shown to the prophet Jeremiah: *Do you not see what these people do in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough to make cakes...* <note>Jeremiah 7:17–18. In this context, the author uses the biblical imagery of a household working together to commit idolatry as an allegory for how the Flesh, World, and Devil work together to corrupt the human will.</note>

## ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL.
<meta>catchword: good</meta>

...they try to bend [God's] will to their own. It is a short commandment that a person should direct his heart. Do you wish to have an upright heart? Do what God wills; do not wish for God to do what you will, etc. This is the mindset of those who are upright in heart, who follow the will of God and not their own. But those who wish to follow God make him the leader and themselves the followers—not themselves the leaders and him the follower. And in all things they find Him good, whether He is correcting, comforting, or testing; whether crowning, purifying, or illuminating, just as the Apostle says: *We know that for those who love God, all things work together for good.* <note>original: "Scimus, quoniam diligentibus Deum, omnia cooperantur in bonum." Romans 8:28.</note>

Look, these are the truest eagle chicks <note>A reference to the medieval belief that young eagles were tested by being forced to stare at the sun; only those who could gaze without blinking were considered legitimate offspring.</note>, who gaze at the sun with fixed eyes, and who seriously apply their minds to the divine will. It is quite different for those who never cease to argue silently with God. At one moment the harshness of the sky displeases them, at another a rainy storm; now they complain of too much cold, now too much heat. Sometimes they feel God does not provide enough for their needs, or that he allows this or that wicked man to prosper, or that he does not punish enemies as they think they should be punished. They are always finding fault and constantly grumbling; God does nothing that they fully approve of. This is that "crooked heart," this is that "self-will," <term>self-will (propria voluntas)<gloss>the human tendency to act according to one's own desires rather than in obedience to God</gloss></term> about which we must listen to Bernard, following Augustine.

Self-will, which subverts the hearts of men and closes the eyes of reason, is a restless evil that, always weighing upon the spirit, meditates on things beyond imagination. And from where do scandals come, from where comes turmoil, if not because we follow our own will? We rashly define in our hearts what we want at the moment, and if it happens to be prohibited or hindered in any way, we are immediately prone to impatience, to grumbling, and to taking offense. We fail to notice that all things work together for good for those who are called to be holy according to His purpose; <note>Romans 8:28.</note> and what seems to us to be a mere accident is actually a certain word from God, indicating His will to us. Let us therefore beware of our own will, as if of the worst and most wicked viper, which alone has the power to condemn our souls.

Such a tree is man; the devil's prompting is the iron, and the human will is the handle.

# BOOK IV.

Although with a mortal heart they might privately desire something that suits their own cause, business, or present necessity for the time being, as soon as they understand and realize that God wills something else, they place that better will before their own. They prefer the will of the Almighty to the will of the weak, and the will of God to the will of man. For as far as God is distant from man, so far is the will of God distant from the will of man.

Augustine speaks elegantly on this: "My pain comes," he says, "and my rest will also come. My tribulation comes, and my purification will also come. Does gold not shine in the goldsmith's furnace? It will shine in the necklace; it will shine in the ornament. Let it, however, endure the furnace, so that, once cleansed of dross <note>The Latin 'sordibus' refers to impurities or waste matter separated during smelting.</note>, it may come into the light. In this furnace, there is the chaff, there is the gold, there is the fire, and the goldsmith blows upon it. In the furnace, the chaff burns while the gold is purified. The former is turned to ashes, while the latter is stripped of its impurities. The World is the furnace, the wicked are the chaff, the just are the gold, tribulation is the fire, and God is the goldsmith. Therefore, I do what the goldsmith wills; I endure where the goldsmith places me. I am commanded to endure; He knows how to purify. Let the chaff burn to heat me and, as it were, consume me; the chaff is turned to ash, but I am freed from filth. Why? Because my soul shall be subject to God."

Behold, the true subjection of the human will to the divine is the source of every good.

The great Abraham is worthy of the highest praise in this regard. For so that it might be witnessed by the World that Abraham did all things according to the decree of the divine will, God—as if changing His own mind several times—wearied the man with various commands that seemed, on the surface, to be contradictory and plainly harsh. But indeed, Abraham was always most obedient to every nod of the divine judgment; he acted with all effort and zeal, and with all his strength, to most generously devote himself and all his possessions to the one and only will of God. 3. In Egypt, in the court of King Pharaoh, he undergoes danger to his life, while his wife faces a threat to her modesty and is taken away from her husband.
4. Because of the continuous quarreling of their servants, he is torn away from his most dear Lot, whom he regarded as a son.
5. In order to restore Lot to freedom after he was captured in war, he leads out a domestic army of home-born servants against four kings.

8. Abimelech, the king of Gerar, again takes his wife from him.
9. He is ordered to drive Hagar with her son Ishmael from his house once more.

BOOK IV.
Q 5

...to themselves <note>The OCR "fefe" is a transcription of "sese," completing the phrase "ad sese" (within themselves) from the previous page.</note> how that province or this one should behave in the face of war and plague, and how these men should conduct themselves against diseases? Can they refuse what God wills? They cannot. Is there therefore no place for defense? There is, provided that God permits it. In what manner did Abraham conduct himself on Mount Moriah <note>The site of the near-sacrifice of Isaac; see Genesis 22.</note> when he was about to sacrifice Isaac? He looked around and saw a ram caught in the thicket; this ram was substituted as a sacrificial victim in place of Isaac. Exactly so should a kingdom afflicted by war, a province infected by plague, or a man tormented by gout <term>podagra: a painful form of inflammatory arthritis, often historically associated with wealthy diets</term> look around for what lawful remedy there may be, and use it to turn away war, remove the plague, or mitigate the gout. If God wills this same thing—that the one be averted, the other removed, and the last mitigated—He will provide the ram; He will supply the remedy to soothe all those things or to restore them to wholeness. But if there is no remedy, or if it does not succeed, it is most clear that God wills that Isaac be sacrificed: that the kingdom be worn down by wars, that the province be exhausted by plague, and that this man be tortured by gout. The reasoning is exactly the same for poverty, disgrace, and all other calamities and miseries. Therefore, where God shows a means of help, Isaac is set free; if not, he must be slaughtered. Therefore, in all these things, the human will should always submit itself most calmly to the divine will. This is to fight against every Mischance and Fortune with golden weapons <note>original: "armis aureis." A metaphorical expression for using the highest virtues or most noble means—in this case, divine submission—to face life's trials.</note>: to think of God, to be subject to God, and in every event, to bend the mind to this...

...pleased him <note>The text likely completes the Latin word 'placuit,' indicating the Bishop’s internal acceptance of the situation.</note>; he approached as if he were about to warm himself, and said: "A hearth is always good, especially for an old man." Let Isaac be sacrificed if a ram is not provided; let the son be immolated if God so commands. Let the house perish, let goods perish, let all things perish, so long as the will of God is done.

### CHAPTER IV.

II. But alas, the fickleness and inconstancy of the human will! That which was just now aligned with God begins again to be its own. *And Jonah was afflicted with a great affliction, and he was angry.* <note>original: "Et affictus est Ionas afflictione magna, & iratus est." He who fits his will to God’s is never so greatly troubled, nor is he ever so deformed by hardships that he bursts into anger and feels indignant toward God. ...one's own will <term>Latin: *propria voluntas*; the theological concept of the human ego acting in isolation from or opposition to God's will</term> does not care; it attends only to what is pleasing and delightful to itself. Whether an action pleases God or not, it regards as exactly the same. *And Jonah went out of the city, and sat over against the East of the city: and he made himself a booth there, and sat under it in the shadow, that he might see what would happen to the city.* <note>Jonah 4:5. Despite the city's repentance, Jonah withdraws to a distance, still hoping to witness the disaster he predicted.</note> This self-will does not yet rest; he deserts the city so that he might more conveniently watch the city's destruction. 

But why does Jonah go out? Why does he not continue to encourage the hearts of the citizens toward constant repentance? What need is there to weave a new dwelling for himself out of ivy? A thousand houses within the city would have welcomed the—by no means unwelcome—preacher of penance. But it pleased his own self-will otherwise; for that will, sometimes not only the most sprawling cities, but the entire circle of the earth is too narrow. Jonah thought that as soon as he left the city, rains of fire would rush down from heaven, and the city would be fundamentally overturned. For God had commanded the prophet to issue this threat: *Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.* <note>Jonah 3:4. In the author's view, Jonah treats God's warning as a personal vindication rather than a conditional call to mercy.</note> For this reason, Jonah places himself in safety; he sits here to see whether God would add no force to His threats—whether He would so easily blot out every injury and spare that most wicked city. 

He waited a long time for a spectacle from heaven. But when all of heaven seemed to take a holiday—when no fires flew, no stones burst forth, and all vengeance seemed to sleep; and when even his delight in the ivy began to wither, as the sun from above...

...who was cast down. But why, my Jonah, do you mourn so greatly for your palace of ivy <note>original: "hederaceum palatium." You did not teach the worm to gnaw, nor the ivy to grow. The Lord gave this to you, and the Lord has taken it away; why are you indignant with the Lord? <note>This echoes the famous patience of Job: "The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away" (Job 1:21).</note> For if the destruction of an ivy shelter is the cause of such great grief, should the overturning of a city that rivals a kingdom not be a cause of grief? Now therefore, my excellent Jonah, conform your will to the divine in every part. The ivy perished? Be willing for it to have perished. Nineveh was saved? Be willing for it to be saved. Nor is there anything for which you should grieve further, except for your own will not being immediately subject to the divine.

III. See, Christians, what it is to belong to one's own judgment and one's own will <term>Latin: "propria voluntas"; the concept of personal desire or ego acting independently of God's guidance</term>, and into how many errors this one thing draws even the holiest of men. We achieve nothing as long as we do not thoroughly conquer our own will. While this personal will stands and opposes the divine, no gifts to God, nor vows, nor prayers, nor sacrifices are pleasing. Fasting is pleasing to God, alms are pleasing, the zeal for praying is pleasing, but only that which is adapted to the divine will. Indeed, one's own will also knows how to distribute alms, institute fasts, and begin prayers, but all these things are more than hateful to God if they are not conformed to the divine will. Augustine, explaining this, says: "Truly, from a perverse will, **lust** <term>lust: from the Latin "libido," referring here to any disordered or intense worldly desire, not limited to the sexual</term> was born; and while lust is served, habit is formed; and while habit is not resisted, necessity is created." By these links, as it were, joined to one another (whence I called it a chain), a harsh servitude held me bound. But the new will which had begun to be in me, that I might worship you freely and desire to enjoy you, O God, was not yet fit to overcome the former will, strengthened by its long duration. Thus my two wills, one old, the other new, the former carnal, the latter spiritual, were in conflict with each other, and by their discord they were **tearing my soul apart** <note>original: "dissipabant animam meam"; literally "were scattering my soul"</note>; and that which was worse, having become ingrained, had more power over me than that which was better but unfamiliar.

Thus when vices pass into character, no more room is left for remedies. For this is the **nature** <note>original: "genius"</note> of all vices: that unless they are cast out of the house as quickly as possible, they can be expelled only with difficulty and rarely once they have grown strong.

<margin>Gregory, Moralia, book 4, chapter 25, after the middle.</margin>
Truly says Gregory: "When a fault has become a habit," he says, "the mind resists it more weakly, even if it desires to resist; for by as many times as it is bound by wicked repetition, it is tied to the mind by just as many chains." It is easy to set right years that are still tender; it is difficult to do so for those grown old. Woe to the pot whose rust is in...

# ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

...was carried about, mobile and unstable through various things, yet persisting firm and unshaken, he was a single man. <note>The author contrasts a person of focused virtue—who remains "one" or "whole"—with the fragmented, shifting nature of most people.</note> Most of us do not act as a single person, and often we are not even "men" at all, being as weak in acts of virtue as we are inconstant. These are the "illustrious" crimes of the **self-will** <term>voluntas propria; the tendency to follow one's own desires rather than God's</term>. <margin>In *Trismegistus*, Book 1, Chapter 8, on the inconstancy of human will <note>Original: "In Trismegisto lib. 1. cap. 8. de humanae voluntatis inconstantia." Therefore, **free will** makes us our own; a bad will makes us the devil’s; a good will makes us God’s. For those, says Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic.</note>, who wished to be their own masters—just like "gods knowing good and evil"—became not only their own masters but also the devil's. Indeed, it is our own will that enslaves us to the devil, not his own power over us. Our will, however, will not be perfect until it is perfectly subjected to its Creator. <margin>Bernard, *On Grace and Free Choice* <note>Original: "Bern. de grat. & lib. arb."</note></margin> Surely, he says, it is better for us not to exist at all than to remain our own. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), a foundational Father of the Church.</note> says of eagles: The chicks of eagles are said to be tested in this way—held in the father's talons and placed against the rays of the sun. The one who gazes firmly at the sun is recognized as a true son; if his sight wavers, he is released from the claw. We lowly little men are more under the judgment of God than a chick is under the eagle’s claw; we depend more upon God than a ray depends on the sun or heat on a fire. God has more power over us than a potter has over clay, and yet we most freely turn away from this Sun of ours, the **Divine Will**. Are we commanded to forgive an enemy? We refuse.

### BOOK IV.

To restrain unbridled lust? We are equally unwilling. To tame uncontrollable anger? We do not wish for this either. To abstain from this or that familiar vice? We "will" it most sluggishly; that is, we modestly "will not." O, you offspring not of eagles, but of owls—who seek not the sun of the divine will, but the darkness of your own! <margin>Blosius, *Spiritual Mirror*, chapter 10, near the end. <note>Original: "Blof. Mon. spirit. ca. 10. fine." Refers to Louis de Blois (1506–1566), a Flemish mystical writer also known as Ludovicus Blosius.</note></margin>
As Louis Blosius relates, Christ, appearing as an intimate friend to a certain holy virgin, said: "I want you to know," He said, "that all the punishments with which men are afflicted in the world consist in the **will** <term>voluntas; the faculty of choice and desire</term>. For if the will were ordered and in harmony with my will, it would in a certain sense be free of punishment. For although the one endowed with this holy and ordered will feels toil and pain, nevertheless, whatever they suffer spontaneously for love of me, they bear as if without punishment. Indeed, they endure it most gladly, considering and knowing it to be my will and my permission that they suffer. Their mind is free in any bodily pain, since their own will is conformed in all things and united to my will. Therefore, when **self-will** <term>voluntas propria; the ego-driven desire that acts independently of God</term> is taken away, the spirit of man is tranquil and enjoys peace."

### Chapter VI.

->*That nothing of self-will is to be retained, both in all arduous and difficult matters, as well as in death itself.*<-

"Here is Rhodes, here is the leap." <note>original: "Hic Rhodus, hîc saltus." A Latin proverb derived from one of Aesop's fables. It means: "Here is the place to prove your claims; act now rather than boasting."</note> In small matters from time to time, we adjust our will to the divine without much difficulty; but in those things that are of weightier importance—in the loss of wealth, honor, or life—here there are evasions and excuses, here are delays and entanglements, here is much stubbornness of a rebellious will. Here our own **WILLING** and **NOT WILLING** stand against God’s **WILLING** and **NOT WILLING**. But why do we wretches struggle in vain? The divine will stands, and it will stand eternally like an immovable rock; we shall not pull it to us, but it pulls us toward itself. We would laugh at someone who, having tied a skiff to a rock, pulled the rope repeatedly and thought the rock was approaching him, when he himself was approaching closer and closer to it. And is our folly not greater? We are bound to that rock of the divine will, yet by pulling and resisting, we want it to obey us, rather than obeying it ourselves.

I. There are those who teach the divine law to both themselves and others, and these indeed consecrate their intellect to God; but where is the **will** <term>voluntas; the faculty of choice and desire</term>, the most precious of all things? This they keep for themselves, having made a division with God—

<vocab>self-will, death, divine will, willing and not willing, divine law</vocab>

<meta>catchword: not</meta>

BOOK IV.

...hardly fair. Long ago, people prayed for one another in this excellent way: <margin>2 Maccabees Chapter 1, verse 3.</margin> *May God do good to you, and give you all a heart to worship him and do his will with a great heart and a willing soul.* These people, however, worship God with an entirely narrow heart and a soul that is not at all willing; they yield to His will in easy matters, but when the dice are cast concerning their wealth, or a point of honor is at stake, or the very pivot of their life turns, they hold most tenaciously to the right of their own will—at this point, they are their own masters. Oh, they are not at all like the **Volones** <term>Volones; in Roman history, these were slaves who, after a great defeat at Cannae, volunteered for military service—a rare act, as slaves were usually barred from the army</term>, who <margin>Livy, Book 3 on the Punic War.</margin> gave their names to military service of their own accord, promising to fight for their masters. For this reason, they were received into citizenship and ordered to be free. 

If those stubborn people, so rebellious against the divine will, would only surrender themselves of their own accord and voluntarily submit their will to that Supreme Will, they would surely obtain the right of heaven, becoming free for all eternity. Among such "volunteers," the Hebrew King David was clearly outstanding: <margin>Psalm 55, verse 13.</margin> *Your vows are upon me, O God,* he said, *which I will render as praises to you.* <note>original: "In me, inquit, sunt Deus vota tua, quæ reddam, laudationes tibi." ### ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

...certainly was one whose name was **What God Wills** <note>original: "Quod vult Deus." This was a common late-antique name, particularly in North Africa, expressing total submission to divine providence.</note>. There was also another of the same name, a Bishop of Carthage, a most holy man, who, together with his clergy, was set adrift by the Arian king **Genseric** <note>Genseric (r. 428–477 AD) was the King of the Vandals who conquered Roman North Africa. Yet, against all hope, he reached Naples and there, as a holy exile, he finished his life. May this be both the name and the sole pursuit of all Christians: **What God Wills**. 

But it is the mark of a malicious man to say "What God Wills" only when nothing laborious or difficult is commanded. He wins every point of praise <note>original: "Ille fert omne punctum," a classical idiom meaning to gain universal approval or to succeed completely.</note> who, when poverty presses, when illness tries him, when disgrace weighs him down, or when death calls, nevertheless proclaims with a most free mind: **What God Wills**. If He wishes wealth, health, reputation, or even life to be taken away—**What God Wills**, let it be done. Such a man does not argue why it must happen now, or why in this place, or why he must die from this particular kind of disease; instead, most prepared for all things, he constantly repeats this one thing:

### ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

...to follow. The body which you now lay aside is a certain worthless garment <note>original: "vile quoddam vestimentum." Blosius uses this metaphor to remind the reader that the physical body is temporary and secondary to the soul.</note>. What is it to you if it rots and is hidden in the earth for a time? Afterward, that very same body of yours will rise again, and then it will be immortal, incorruptible, glorious, and shining. One must also consider how resigned and willing to die the ancient righteous ones were—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and others like them—even when the gate of the heavenly kingdom was not yet open. Hence, at the end of Deuteronomy we read that the Lord said to Moses: *Go up into this mountain,* etc., *and see the land of Canaan which I shall give to the children of Israel to possess, and die on the mountain.* <note>original: "Ascende in montem istum... & morere in monte." This refers to Deuteronomy 32:49-50.</note> 

See with what a resigned soul, according to God’s good pleasure, Moses, the friend of the Most High, received death. He did not indeed cross over to that visible land, but was received into an invisible and better one—namely, into the secret bosom of peace and the limbo <term>Limbo: Specifically the "Limbo of the Fathers" (Limbus Patrum), the place where the souls of the righteous were said to wait before the Resurrection of Christ opened the gates of Heaven.</term> in which the souls of the righteous then rested in great tranquility. Now, however, the entrance to the heavenly homeland has been opened for the righteous through Christ the Lord.

Therefore, my dear Christian, when you feel death nearby—indeed, even before you feel it—join your will as perfectly as possible with the divine will, and commit yourself entirely to it: think and speak of nothing else than this: *When it pleases the Lord.* <note>original: "Quando Domino visum." A phrase expressing total submission to God's timing for one's death.</note>

...yourself, setting aside all partiality; then you will feel and confess that none of these desirable and dear things are truly useful to you, unless you have armed yourself against the fickleness of chance and the events that follow from it. You must do this by saying frequently and without complaint amidst every loss: *It seemed otherwise to God.* <note>original: "Deo aliter visum est." This is a famous quotation from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (Book 2, line 428). While Virgil used it to express the inscrutability of the gods, the author repurposes it here as a formula for Christian resignation.</note> You shall say: "Until now, I thought I would live longer, but *it seemed otherwise to God*, and it was well that it so seemed." Once your own will has been transformed into the Divine will, all things will become easy for you. 

For just as an evil man turns everything into evil, even those things which appear to be for the best; so a righteous and upright man corrects the crooked things of life. He softens the hard and the rough through the <term>science of enduring</term> <note>original: "ferendi scientia." The author treats the ability to bear suffering not just as a feeling, but as a systematic discipline or "science" to be mastered.</note>. Such a man receives prosperity gratefully and modestly, and meets adversity with constancy and bravery. Being so devoted to the Divine will, he never curses bad outcomes, nor does he ever receive accidents with a gloomy spirit. Believing himself to be a citizen and a soldier of the universe, <note>The author adopts the Stoic concept of the *Cosmopolis*, where a person views themselves as part of a larger universal order, owing duty to the whole rather than just their own interests.</note> he undergoes labors as if they were commanded of him. Whatever happens, he does not reject it as an evil or as something cast upon him by mere chance, but as something specifically delegated to him. "Whatever this may be," he says, "it is mine. It is rough, it is hard: let us apply ourselves to the task and not complain about God's providence." As Epictetus says: <margin>*Epictetus, Handbook, chapter 79, or the last.*</margin> "If it should so please the gods, so let it be."

Referring to St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note>—and earned more merit for himself with only a few little words than with all his most generous acts of charity. For when Job, afflicted on all sides, said: *As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; Blessed be the name of the Lord* <note>Job 1:21. The author highlights that Job's verbal acceptance of his suffering was more spiritually significant than his previous wealth and philanthropy.</note>, he proved himself more to the Divine will than when he distributed the most liberal alms. For, as we learn from Saint Bonaventure <margin>Bonaventure, *On the Grace of Virtues*, chapter 24; Psalm 15, verse 2.</margin>: It is more perfect to endure adversity patiently than to sweat over good works. For God has no need of our goods.

Whoever, therefore, sincerely seeks the Divine will, whether they be healthy or sick, considers it all the same, since the will of God is our entire good. In sickness, moreover, one should trust the physician and the medicines in such a way that, meanwhile, all trust is placed in God's providence and will. Because King Asa did not do this, he was rightly rebuked: for in his illness he did not seek the Lord, but rather trusted in the art of physicians. <note>2 Chronicles 16:12. Asa is a biblical king of Judah often cited in moral literature as a warning against placing secular science above spiritual faith.</note> Hezekiah did better, who attributed the cure of his disease not to the figs, nor to the one applying them, but to God. <note>2 Kings 20. Hezekiah was healed of a life-threatening boil after a poultice of figs was applied, but the author emphasizes his prayer over the physical remedy.</note> But if the medicines do no good, or if the physician does not perceive the strength of the disease, or...

### A brief explanation of the following image.

To endure *adversity* PATIENTLY & CONSTANTLY; to trust in God as *most generously* as possible in all things—this, finally, is <term>Christian nobility<note>In this context, "nobility" refers to a spiritual excellence or a "high-born" soul that proves its character through virtue rather than social rank.</note></term>. In this matter, all the holy Angels provide the greatest assistance; by their prayers and examples, we are kindled toward the fullest agreement with the divine will. Moses also teaches us this—a man most gentle, and tolerant of injuries beyond what can be expressed. To this, the very will of God calls the human heart: RISE UP, HASTEN <note>original: "SURGE, PROPERA." A reference to the Song of Solomon 2:10, often used in mystical literature to describe God summoning the soul into a deeper relationship.</note>, first to obedience, and then to an embrace. It is for man to respond as promptly as possible: BEHOLD, I AM HERE <note>original: "ECCE ADSUM." This is the classic biblical response of readiness and availability to God, famously spoken by Abraham, Isaiah, and the Virgin Mary.</note>, prepared for both; most ready both to do and to endure all things: BEHOLD, I am here. This, at last, is the most blessed marriage of the Divine and human will; this is heaven outside of heaven, nor is there any surer or more secure path to paradise. The rest, my reader, regarding the explanation of the images, you will find at the start of the final chapter.

## CHAPTER I.

->*That the conforming of the human will to the divine cannot exist without great confidence in God.*<-

The offering of oneself <note>original: "oblatio sui"</note> to the divine judgment will never be complete unless we trust God most highly in all things. For how can I agree with another in all matters if I do not trust him? And how can I trust someone whom I do not believe will care for my affairs faithfully or with concern? Therefore, we must now discuss the placing of our confidence in God.

### III.

Finally, what does Christ instill and urge in so many ways, if not this one Trust in God? How varied are the arguments this divine Teacher uses—from little birds, from tiny flowers, from the hairs of one’s head, and even from the idolaters themselves—to persuade us of this trust? Thus, placing ravens, lilies, and sparrows before our eyes: "Consider the ravens," He says, "for they do not sow, nor do they reap; they have no storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. How much more are you worth than they? Who among you by thinking can add a single cubit <note>A biblical unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> to his stature? If then you cannot do even the smallest thing, why are you anxious about the rest?"

V. And indeed, when discussing prayers, Bernard says that the prayer of many is either timid, lukewarm, or rash. A timid prayer, he says, does not penetrate heaven, because immoderate fear restricts the soul so that the prayer—I will not say it cannot ascend—cannot even proceed. A lukewarm prayer, however, grows faint and fails during its ascent because it lacks vigor. For a rash prayer ascends, but it bounces back; it is resisted, and not only does it fail to obtain grace, but it even deserves offense.
