...that he has not prayed in vain, and that he will certainly obtain other and better things.

**V.** If God does not cease to strike His children, and exercises them with one calamity after another, He is doing exactly what any excellent father or mother would do. When parents punish their children with rods, they are often accustomed to ask after one or two lashes: "Do you intend to repeat this fault?" If the child remains silent while being struck, the father continues to strike; if the stubborn boy does not yet respond, the father persists in the beating, asking again and again: "Well? Do you want to avoid repeating the fault?" He urges this for as long as it takes until the son says: "I will not repeat the fault." Only then does the parent say: "Go now, and take care that you do not repeat this mistake." In this same way, God is accustomed to punish us and to ask: "Do you wish to submit yourself fully to my will, and to trust me in all things?" Because we either remain stubbornly silent, or we do not answer the divine will with a serious intent to obey, God often continues the lashes. He expects nothing else from us than that we say from our heart: "I am willing, my Father, I am willing to obey your will in all things; what would you have me do?"

after the middle.

> Lord, what would you have me do? <note>original: "Domine quid me vis facere?" This is the question asked by the Apostle Paul during his conversion on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:6).</note> O brief word—yet full, living, effective, and worthy of all acceptance. <note>original: "dignum omni acceptione," a phrase borrowed from 1 Timothy 1:15.</note>

How few are found in this state of perfect obedience, who have so cast aside their own will that they do not even possess their own <unclear>heart</unclear>, so that it is not what they themselves want, but what...

### BOOK V.

...what the Lord wants, they should seek at every hour, saying without ceasing: *Lord, what do you want me to do?* <note>original Latin: *Domine quid me vis facere?* These are the words of Saul of Tarsus—the future Apostle Paul—during his miraculous conversion on the road to Damascus in Acts 9:6.</note> Alas, we have more imitators of that blind man from the Gospel than of the new Apostle. "What do you want (says the Lord to that blind man) that I should do for you?" <note>original Latin: *Quid vis ut faciam tibi?* This refers to the blind man Bartimaeus in Mark 10:51 and Luke 18:41, to whom Jesus offers a miracle by asking what the man desires.</note> How great is your mercy, Lord, how great is your condescension! Does the Lord thus ask so that He might do the will of His servant? Truly that blind man, because he did not consider [the weight of this], did not tremble, did not cry out: "Far be it from this, Lord! Rather, you say what you would have me do." For thus it is fitting, thus it is entirely worthy: not that my will be sought and done by you, but that your will be sought and done by me. Thus indeed, the faint-heartedness and perversity of many until today requires that it must be asked of them: "What do you want me to do for you?" while they themselves do not ask: "Lord, what do you want me to do?"

Furthermore, this **Trust** in God of which we speak will not stand for long unless **Patience** strengthens it and **Perseverance** firms it. In the temple of Solomon there were two columns, of which one was called **Jachin** and the other **Boaz**. <note>In the Old Testament, these two bronze pillars stood at the porch of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 7:21). <margin>Psalm 124, verse 1a</margin>

# ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL, CHAPTER IV.

## *With What Great Trust in God All the Saints Were Endowed.*

The true nobility of Christian blood is to trust in God during difficult trials and to rely on Him alone. This spirit is noble and generous, great and exalted—one that trusts God most when facing the greatest calamity. From this most noble lineage, many of the holiest men have emerged.

<margin>Romans, chapter 4, verse 18.</margin>
I. I shall pass over Abraham, who, relying on God, *against hope believed in hope; he did not waver regarding the promise of God through distrust, but was strengthened by faith, giving glory to God; knowing most fully that whatever He promised, He is also powerful to perform.* <note>original Latin: *contra spem in spem credidit...* This quote from Romans 4:18-21 highlights Abraham’s faith that God would provide him a son despite his advanced age.</note> He did not refuse to sacrifice his only-begotten son to the divine will, and with three hundred and eighteen servants, he attacked and defeated four kings with the greatest trust in God. I shall also pass over Joseph, the deputy of Egypt, who, though so often cast down into extreme distress, nevertheless did not lose heart, for his heart was full of trust in the Lord. What wonders did Moses not perform, leaning upon God? He enclosed the entire armies of Egypt in a single grave in the sea. In the war against the Amalekites, he held a staff in place of any heavy artillery <note>original Latin: *curuli tormento*. A *tormentum* was a Roman siege engine or catapult. <margin>Exodus, chapter 17, verse 9.</margin>
he spoke to the commander <note>original Latin: *Imperatorem*. This refers to Joshua, who led the Israelite army while Moses prayed on the hill during the battle.</note>: "Choose men," he said, "and fight against Amalek; tomorrow I will stand on the peak of the hill, holding the rod of God."

From this, he was called PETER OF THE FIRE <note>original: "PETRVS IGNEVS"</note>. Although this man was descended from the most noble lineage of the Aldobrandini, he was nevertheless of such a submissive spirit and so trusting in God that, at the command of his superior Gualbert, he did not refuse to act as a shepherd of the flock. But because virtue is accustomed to stand out even from the lowest positions, Peter was called from the flock, and from the shepherd’s crook to the mitre <note>original: "tiaram"; used here generally to denote high ecclesiastical office</note>; he served as a Provost, then as an Abbot; from there he was chosen as a Bishop, and after that as a Cardinal.

IV. Generally, it can be affirmed of all men and women who excel in the holiness of life:

> *Their heart was having trust in the Lord.*

Nor should the following be wrapped in silence. *Frederick II, Duke of Saxony*, surnamed *the Gentle* <note>original: *Placidus*</note>, died in the Year of Christ 1464. This prince, some years before his death, began a dispute—and eventually a war—against the Prelate of *Magdeburg*, *Frederick*, of the lineage of the Counts [of Beichlingen]. So that he might conduct the war more prudently and that everything might proceed more successfully, he sent a spy to learn about the enemy’s military preparations and plans. It was done: once everything had been scouted, it was reported back that no suitable preparations for war were being made, nor were soldiers being recruited. Furthermore, the Prelate had said that he would entrust his cause to God, who would take up arms for His servant. When the *Elector* <note>A Prince-Elector (Kurfürst) was one of the high-ranking members of the Holy Roman Empire who elected the Emperor.</note> heard this, he said: "Let someone else be so mad as to wage war against one who trusts that he will be superior in his cause with God as his defender." The Prelate is to be praised for relying on the protection of God; and the Prince is to be praised for laying down his arms out of fear of having God as an adversary.

At last, when the ship was brought into harbor, Elzéar sternly rebuked some of his followers because they had shown clearly enough by their shouts and tears that they relied on very little trust in God and shrunk too much from death. 

Afterward, however, his wife Delphine <note>Saint Delphine of Glandèves (1284–1358), who lived in a virginal marriage with Elzéar; both were renowned for their sanctity.</note> asked Elzéar in private whether he alone, in such immediate danger, had ceased to be human, and had not feared a death so close at hand? To her he said: "I handed myself over entirely to the divine will, prepared that, if everyone else were kept safe, I alone would be swallowed by the waves." For God is not richer in promises than He is in deeds. He even promised that mountains would be moved and the dead called back to life. Therefore, let a man dare to hope for greater things; God will bestow what He is capable of.

# BOOK V.

<margin>
Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 5, near the beginning.
</margin>
For, as Clement of Alexandria <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150–215 AD), a Christian theologian who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria and sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> rightly says: "There are," he says, "certain questions which deserve to be punished: such as seeking proofs for whether there is a Providence, when divine Providence is manifest from the sight of all things that are seen, which are established by art and wisdom." Therefore, Providence exists.

<margin>
Theophilus Raynaud demonstrates this with the most illustrious arguments and testimonies in his *Natural Theology*, distinction 8, question 3, page 893 in my edition.
</margin>
I. But what is providence? Boëthius* says: It is the divine reason itself, established in the supreme Ruler, which disposes all things. Damascene ‡ speaks best on this matter: "Providence," he says, "is the will of God, through which all things are appropriately and suitably governed." We shall understand the matter thus: God saw from eternity by what means every created thing could attain its end; at the same time, He also saw all the impediments that would occur in attaining that end. Then, this same most excellent God, by His most holy will, chose those aids to be supplied through which all people might be led to their end in the best possible way. Indeed, He proposed these from the very birth of the world, and brought them into effect through His immense power. Thus, divine Providence, as Dorotheus <note>Likely Dorotheus of Gaza (6th century), a monk and abbot whose teachings on spiritual direction were highly influential in the Christian East and West.</note> speaks, is the source of all good things. All the crowds of philosophers have acknowledged this. Hence those sayings: *Follow God*; *Do not fight against the Gods*; *That is a care for those above*; *Jupiter will see to it*; *This lies on the knees* <note>original: "Hoc in genibus," referring to the classical Greek and Latin idiom "it lies on the knees of the gods," meaning the outcome is beyond human control and rests with the divine.</note>

This rule is most certain. Wisdom cries out: "He himself made both the small and the great, and He has equal care for all."

However, so that we may fix the knowledge of divine Providence in our deepest minds, we lay this as the foundation: Nothing in the whole world happens by chance or accident. If we examine things only according to our own foresight or knowledge, we will see many things happen by some impulse and by "luck of the draw"; but if we look to the Divine Intelligence, nothing happens by chance. For the Divine Intelligence is infinite, and extends itself without any limit to everything that can be understood. At one and the same point in time, in a single blink of an eye, it perceives and sees through all the depths and recesses of heaven, earth, sea, and the underworld.

### BOOK V.

...God was from eternity. Thus, in all things, the most wonderful providence of divine governance shines forth, which not only presides over all things, but is among them—indeed, is within them. We, who are blind, think many things happen by chance, yet all these things proceed from the eternal counsel and providence of God.

<margin>Augustine, on Psalm 9, after the middle section.</margin>
II. Augustine says most wisely: "And so let all things be referred to the rule of divine providence, which fools think happen as if by chance, at random, and by no divine administration." The matter will be made clear by an example: A master <note>original: "Herus," meaning the head of a household or employer</note> sends two of his servants, who are unaware of their master's plan, by different paths to exactly the same place. Here, for one to run into the other is a matter of "chance" to the servants, but not to the master. In the same way, for a treasure to be found by a poor digger is indeed "chance" for that poor man, but not for God, who willed the riches to be hidden there so that this very laborer, digging in that spot, might find them and become wealthy—not by chance, but by the fatherly providence of God. To God, nothing at all is accidental. Therefore:

**Paphnutius** <note>An Egyptian desert monk of the 4th century known for his asceticism and wisdom.</note> was once asked what the cause was that some people make progress while others fail, even when they are under the same teacher; why do some fall while others stand firm? He replied: "Whatever happens occurs either by **God’s good pleasure** <term>Latin: beneplacitum; refers to things God actively wills, such as acts of virtue</term> or by **God’s permission** <term>Latin: permissio; refers to God allowing free will to result in evil or suffering without being the cause of it</term>." He explained that all things joined with virtue happen according to God’s good pleasure, but other things which are allied with vice—bringing losses and injuries upon the world—happen by God’s permission. But why does God permit such great and frequent evils? At this point, **Plato** <note>The Greek philosopher; the author suggests that even classical philosophy recognizes the limits of human reason before divine mystery.</note> bids us be silent: *God’s judgments are a great abyss.* <note>original: "judicia Dei abyssus multa"; a reference to Psalm 36:6, suggesting God's plans are as deep and mysterious as the ocean.</note> This was best understood by the one who said:

Most remarkably, **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan and a key Doctor of the Church.</note> said: *The Lord sleeps for the lukewarm, but watches over the perfect.* This is not because He forgets those whom He warns, rebukes, stirs, or punishes, but rather because He demonstrates His providence toward His own people in singular ways and with many proofs. When **Jacob** was asked by his
<margin>Genesis, chapter 33, verse 5.</margin>
brother about his company, he replied: "These are the children whom God has graciously given to me, your servant." Thus, he calmly taught him (says **Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), known for his eloquent preaching and reflections on divine care.</note>) how great God's providence had been toward him. The upright are cared for by God as friends and as sons, but the wicked are treated as mere chattels and servants. And although God is almost reluctant to disturb the order of nature, He nevertheless overturns it thousands and thousands of times for the sake of His friends. From this come the deeds of the Saints, so admirable for their many wonders and miracles.

This wonderful Providence of God is in the manner of—

## CHAPTER VII.

->*How great the Providence of God is regarding the necessities of life.*<-

Truly all things are in the hand of God; yet someone has well said that God keeps three keys with Himself, which He entrusts to no one: one key to bring forth rains, winds, snows, and other such offspring of the air; a second key to unlock the tombs and call the dead back to life; and a third for the storehouse <note>original: "penu," referring to a household's inner storeroom or larder.</note> and every kind of nourishment. But if God should shut these storerooms, who shall open them? Therefore, God is the steward and distributor <note>original: "promus condus." In a Roman household, the *promus condus* was the slave in charge of the cellar and provisions, responsible for both storing and giving out supplies.</note> of all things: from Him must be obtained whatever is necessary for leading this life.

He who does not trust God in these fleeting <note>original: "caducis," referring to things that fall away or perish easily.</note> things, how much less will he trust Him in other matters regarding eternity? And the first argument which Christ used against our lack of trust <note>original: "diffidentiam"</note> is this: "Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?" Here, with the most powerful arguments, He removes from the mind that most harmful worry concerning clothing and food, and teaches that one must trust solely in the nourishing <note>original: "alma," suggesting a motherly, life-giving care.</note> providence of God. For if God is so provident and generous in those things that seem more complex <note>original: "operosiora." The author argues that if God performed the "harder" task of creating life, the "easier" task of providing clothes is guaranteed.</note>, why do we accuse God of forgetfulness or neglect in other matters that are less complex? If He gave the body, why would He deny the clothing? To him who gives a horse, why would he withhold the bridle? Is not life more precious than that by which life is nourished, and the body more excellent than that by which the body is covered? Certainly. Therefore, He who gave life and a body to us when we were not worrying at all—indeed, when we did not even exist in the nature of things—will undoubtedly also give those things by which life and body are to be sustained, especially since He Himself willed that life and the body should have need of these things. If, therefore, He gave the greater things of His own accord, He has declared that He is both able and willing to give the lesser things as well. However, He will give them not to those of us who are idle—for He did not create us for idleness—but to those free from worry, for God wants this weight of worry to be cast upon Himself.

To make this providence perfectly clear, He does not bring up the feeding of Israel in the desert for forty years; He does not praise Elijah being fed by ravens; instead, He presents brute animals—and not lions, bears, elephants, or other such large creatures, which are also fed by divine power, but the smallest of animals: little birds. Since they spend almost all their time singing and take their food as if by chance, they seem most free from worry. And should man, who is worth more than countless little birds and recognizes God not only as Lord but as Father, be so distressed in his soul?

The Flood <note>The Great Flood of Genesis, often attributed in theological commentary to the moral decay resulting from idleness and plenty.</note> testifies to this, the beginnings of which were luxury and idleness, leading to a life for all that was full of lusts and a deadened sense of shame. Behold, how great is God's providence, which draws men from lasciviousness to labor through poverty; labor rouses the best in us. Whatever beauty we discern anywhere has been worked out by those who did not abound in money and were therefore forced to sell their labors.

To which Augustine responds excellently: "Hope," he says, "has not yet arrived at the reality; and an egg is something, but it is not yet a chick." <note>original: "Spes nondum pervenit ad rem; & ovum est aliquid, sed nondum est pullus." Augustine uses this metaphor to explain that hope is the beginning of a thing, but not yet its fulfillment.</note>

IV. They say there was a beggar who, when he saw his knapsack already filled and stuffed everywhere with bread, used to say: *Now I hope*. We are very similar to this beggar; for we only have "hope" when we believe we have been magnificently provided for many years to come. Truly, we conceive only as much hope as we see of present wealth. It was far different for John the Patriarch of Alexandria <note>Saint John the Almsgiver (c. 550–619 AD), the Eastern Orthodox Patriarch of Alexandria famous for his extreme charity and trust in God.</note>, who through true confidence depended entirely on divine providence, by which single thing he applied an easy remedy to the greatest calamities. It happened that thirteen grain ships, each of which held ten thousand <term>modii</term> <note>A *modius* was a Roman dry measure, approximately 2 gallons or 8.7 liters. Ten thousand modii would be a massive cargo of grain.</note>, were sunk in the sea. Nearly half of the citizens of Alexandria were affected by this huge loss; therefore, the sailors and others fled to the sanctuary of Alexandria. To them John soon sent a note, in which only this was...

...restrained, he led a most continent life upon a solitary rock. This was the entirety of his provisions and the manner of his service. The evil spirit <note>original: *cacodæmon*</note> took this abstinence poorly. Therefore, seizing an opportunity while the holy man was poured out in prayer upon his knees, a raven flew down, overturned the water-jar with its feet, and carried away the bread in its beak; thus, all the provisions for the three-day period were lost.

How did *Amatus* respond to these things? Perhaps by being indignant at the raven, or by devoting the predatory bird to every curse, or by hurling atrocious words against the providence of God, or by execrating these machinations of the devil? *Amatus* did none of these things: such complaints are our songs, not his. Instead, lifting his hands and his mind to heaven, he said: "I give thanks to you, Lord JESUS, because it pleases your most holy will that I be exercised by a longer fast. I know this will be useful to me, since nothing is done in this world without your providence."

Listen, you complainers and unbelievers: Nothing in this world is done without divine providence, without which not even a tiny leaf falls from a tree. And yet you think that houses are burned, ships are sunk, fortunes are snatched away, and reputations are violated while this providence is drowsy or sleeping? Even the idolaters <term>idolaters</term><note>Meaning the pagan philosophers of antiquity.</note> themselves perceived things more correctly; for whichever of them possessed any measure of wisdom or sanity held that human affairs were by no means governed by blind or rash chance...

Therefore, says Seneca, everything must be endured bravely, because all things do not fall upon us by chance, as we suppose, but they arrive by design. And indeed, they come from God; why then do we feel indignation and complain?

V. We are led to meditate on this same providence with a steady mind by almost daily examples. Not long ago, a religious man in Valencia <note>original: *Valentia*; a city in Spain</note> set out on a journey of nine miles. Before he had finished the path, he was overcome with total exhaustion from the heat, hunger, and thirst. He cast himself down under a pear tree <term>pear tree</term><note>Latin: *pirus*</note> and began to pray. As he repeated his prayers, he spotted a rather large pear at the very top of the tree. At that same moment, a traveler <term>traveler</term><note>Latin: *viator*</note> passing by spoke to the man fainting under the tree. When he heard what cause delayed his journey, he drew out a large loaf of white bread, cut off a portion, and gave it to the man to restore his strength. 

We certainly believe these things; we know that countless <note>original: *sexcenta*, literally "six hundred," a common Latin idiom for an infinite or very large number</note> such events occur, and we have experienced similar things ourselves. Nevertheless, our trust in divine providence is often so small that unless our purses <term>purses</term><note>Latin: *marsupia*</note>, chests, larders, cellars, and granaries are stuffed full of every necessity, our soul lies empty of hope. Only when we see a money-bag <term>money-bag</term><note>Latin: *crumena*</note> stuffed with coins do we finally have hope. O you of poor vision!

<header>ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL</header>

Trust in God is most true when hope is squeezed into a narrow place and struggles against the most difficult circumstances. We see the evils we suffer, but we do not yet see the glory for which we suffer; the greater the torment, the greater the glory will be.

Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), a hugely influential theologian and church historian.</note> tells us that the blessed Maesimas <note>A Syrian ascetic known for his hospitality; the story refers to a miracle similar to the widow's oil in the Bible.</note> had two large jars, one for wheat and the other for oil. From these, he would distribute most generously to the poor, yet the jars never ran empty. God likewise has two "jars": one is filled with grain and everything necessary for life, and the other is overflowing and brimming with mercy, generosity, and providence. Neither can ever be exhausted. We must run back to these two storehouses <term>storehouses</term><note>Latin: *gazophylacia*, originally referring to a treasury or a place for keeping offerings in a temple.</note> when our own meager possessions <note>original: *reculæ nostræ*</note> are sighing at the bottom of the barrel. We need only learn this one thing well: **TO TRUST IN GOD**, and to commit ourselves entirely to His most holy will.

### I.
King Saul sought the blood and the life of David with perpetual snares. It was in vain: God protected him. But when David was hiding in the wilderness of Maon, Saul soon arrived, and with a large body of soldiers he hemmed David in **like a crown** <note>original: *in modum coronae*; this describes a military maneuver where troops encircle a target from all sides.</note> so that there was no place for escape, and indeed no room for hope. David was thought of as a wild beast surrounded by a hunting net and dogs. At this point, David's situation seemed most desperate: Saul, already nearly the victor, was looming directly over his head; the lion already seemed to hold the prey in its jaws. 
<margin>1 Kings, chapter 23, verse 25. <note>In modern English Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 23.</note></margin>

Thus David, after every reason for despair, while already hanging in the claws of a most ferocious tiger, was suddenly released and set free: God protected him. In this way, divine providence most sweetly eluded all the snares of the wicked king. It is not, however, a wonder...

...mercy, you would simultaneously take away the ransom <note>original: *lytrum*; a term derived from Greek referring to the price paid for redemption</note> of the human race: the blood and death of Christ. Take away the devils, and the contests, victories, and rewards will largely cease. Take away the tyrants; where then will the martyrs be? This is the habit of divine providence: to use not only good things, but even evil things for the sake of the good. Certainly, if you look at the nature of the act, the selling of Joseph was effectively guided by God; yet the wickedness hidden within that act came from the most evil will of his brothers. However, God provided many means by which He might correct this entire injury. 

<margin>Gregory, *Moralia*, book 6, chapter 14.</margin> 

Gregory speaks beautifully here: "Behold," he says, "how divine power catches the wise in their very own wisdom! Joseph was sold for this reason: so that he would not be bowed down to; yet he was bowed down to <note>The Latin *adoraretur* refers to the prophetic dreams in Genesis where Joseph's brothers bowed to him, which they tried to prevent by selling him.</note> precisely because he was sold." The same happened to Moses. For the man whom King Pharaoh had destined for death, Pharaoh's daughter—at God's instigation—entrusted to herself to be raised. In your own court, Pharaoh, you are forced to nourish the one who is destined to avenge those whom you so extremely persecute. 

Augustine says: "A new miracle! The daughter of a murderer <note>original: *parricidæ*; while literally "parricide," it here refers to Pharaoh as a tyrant and killer of the Hebrew infants.</note> performed a supreme work of mercy."

### ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

...[Mo]negund <note>Saint Monegund (d. 570) was a Frankish woman who became a hermit and healer after the death of her daughters. She is a primary figure in Gregory of Tours' hagiographies.</note>, who had daughters of excellent beauty. Upon them, their mother bestowed all her care and love—at that time, however, she was not very pious. It pleased divine providence to remove this "enticement to sin" <note>original: *peccandi illecebram*; the author suggests her excessive worldly attachment to her children was a distraction from her spiritual duties.</note>. Thus, both daughters were taken away by a premature death. The mother, surviving her own funeral <note>original: *suo ipsa funeri velut superstes*; a poetic way of saying she felt dead inside after her children's burial.</note>, as it were, began to hate all life: she tore her hair, scratched her cheeks, rejected all comfort for her grief, and wished for nothing else than to follow her daughters as quickly as possible into death. 

After her grief had been somewhat drained by tears, and as her mourning was now subsiding, Monegund came to her senses. "Am I not," she said, "remarkably foolish for protesting divine providence so stubbornly? What am I doing? Did I not know that I had given birth to mortal daughters? Were they born for this: that they could not die? The Mother of God, the Son of God, and even those humans most dear to God die—and am I indignant that my daughters have ceased to live? Perhaps they died so that they might not fall into vice <note>original: *ne succumberent vitiis*; a common theme in historical theology—that a premature death might be a mercy to prevent a soul from later falling into sin.</note>. Why then do I assault God with my complaints—He who can wish for nothing evil? Why do I not end this foolish lamentation and settle myself entirely within the bosom of divine will and providence?" 

So she said, and so she did. She commanded the world to keep its business, while she shut herself in a small house with a little servant girl, intending to serve God from then on with every effort. That this change of life pleased the Powers Above was made manifest by miracles.

### BOOK V

It is of such great value to entrust oneself completely to divine providence. Saint Augustine said most truly: "He who had care for you before you even existed, how shall He not have care for you now that you are exactly what He willed you to be?" <note>original: "Qui habuit curam tui antequam esses, quomodo non habebit curam tui, cum jam hoc es, quod voluit ut esses?" IV. Robert <note>Saint Robert of Molesme (c. 1028–1111) was one of the founders of the Cistercian Order, known for his strict adherence to monastic poverty.</note>, the first abbot of Molesme, was a most devoted practitioner of divine providence; he gave whatever he could to the poor. It happened once that he ordered two loaves of bread to be given to two beggars waiting at the gates. However, the <term>steward</term> <note>original: *oeconomus*; the monk responsible for the monastery's material goods and food supplies.</note> opposed him, saying that the remaining supply of grain would not even be enough for their own lunch. "What, then," asked Robert, "shall we eat for lunch?" "I do not know," the steward replied. The holy man suspected that something was being hidden away through a poorly-judged stinginess. Therefore, after the religious service was finished and the signal was given to come to the table, the abbot asked from where the bread had been brought. "I saved a few for ourselves," said the <term>provisioner</term> <note>original: *obsonator*; the person in charge of food preparation or purchasing.</note>. Robert, becoming righteously incensed, ordered all the loaves to be gathered into a basket and immediately carried outside to the beggars. Turning to his own monks, he said: "Lest the rebellion of disobedience and distrust spread further in our house, fasting and hunger shall teach us to trust in God." Robert wanted all his followers to depend entirely on the most generous providence of God, just as an infant depends on its mother's strength. The best medicine for wicked <term>parsimony</term> <note>meaning extreme stinginess or greed.</note> is <term>inedia</term> <note>fasting or a lack of food.</note>.

The companion then tasted this "honeyed" porridge with the tips of his lips and immediately fell at the old man's knees. "I have killed you, father!" he said. "And why, I beseech you, did you confirm my reckless thoughtlessness with your silence?" 

To which the old man replied: "Do not be distressed in your soul, my son; for if God had willed that I eat honey, you certainly would have poured honey into the food."

...he knew that if God had wished honey to be eaten by him, He would not have permitted his companion to fall into error, or—which is equally easy for God—He would have turned that most foul-smelling oil into a honeyed liquid.

So behaves the person who recognizes Divine Providence in all things; he does not interpret everything in the worst possible way, nor does he seek someone to blame for his misfortune, but rather refers the sins of men back to God's Providence. Whatever happens, he lightens the burden by interpreting it with kindness.

**V.** At this point, Reader, I would wish for one thing to be grasped by you with the utmost clarity <note>original: *enuclearissimè*; literally "to the heart of the nut," meaning with great precision and detail.</note>. It is a saying of Jerome: "All things are governed by the providence of God, and often what is thought to be punishment, is actually medicine." <note>St. Jerome (c. 342–420 AD) was a foundational Christian scholar best known for translating the Bible into Latin. Here he suggests that life's hardships are intended by God to heal the soul rather than simply to punish it.</note> In this, a wonderful thing must be observed: that Divine Providence allows each thing to be carried along by its own natural motions until a certain time. For this is the custom of Divine Providence: that gradually and through the passing of time, it leads each thing to its destined ends; for it organizes the smallest matters just as much as the greatest.

<margin>Epictetus, *Enchiridion* chapters 1, 30, and 78, 79.</margin>
For that reason, Epictetus—the "sun" of the philosophers—said most excellently: "Do not demand that the things which happen should happen according to your own choice; but if you are wise, wish for things to happen exactly as they do happen." <note>Epictetus (c. 50–135 AD) was a Greek Stoic philosopher. His *Enchiridion* (Manual) taught that peace is found by focusing only on what is within our control and accepting everything else as the work of fate or God.</note> This is a Christian, divine teaching: *Wish for things to happen exactly as they do happen.*

<margin>Basil, *To Eustathius*.</margin>
Basil spoke in a very similar way: "Since," he says, "things do not turn out as we wish, let us wish for them just as they do turn out." <note>St. Basil the Great (330–379 AD) was a bishop and theologian who helped shape early Christian monasticism and the doctrine of the Trinity.</note> 

<margin>Nilus, chapter 29, *On Prayer*.</margin>
In exactly the same way, Abbot Nilus said: "Do not pray," he says, "that the things you wish for may happen, but rather pray, as you have learned to pray, that [Your will] be done..." <note>Nilus of Sinai (died c. 430 AD) was a prolific writer on the spiritual life. He refers here to the Lord’s Prayer: "Thy will be done."</note>

## CHAPTER IX.

-> *How great the Providence of God is toward friends as well as enemies.* <-

There is an old fable <term>apologue: a moral story or allegory</term> which presents divine Providence in this way. A little boy was playing among the flowers by a small stream; at last, tired out by his childish running about, he sat down in a dangerous spot near the water and fell asleep. Soon Fortune <note>Fortune is personified here as a goddess or force of chance.</note> arrived, and scolding the sleeping boy, she said: "Look, you poor little thing, how easy it is to slip from here into the water. Get up, and move away from the nearby danger, lest if any evil happens to you, everyone shifts the blame onto me; and they might say that not you, but I—who neglected you while you slept—was the one sleeping." This was beautifully devised to assert the providence of God. Among all Christians, it is well established what the psalmist proclaimed:

### BOOK V.

<margin>Exodus chapter 16, verse 6.</margin>
[Moses] and Aaron once proclaimed: *In the evening you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord.* <note>original: "Vespere scietis quod Dominus eduxerit vos de terra Ægypti, & mane videbitis gloriam Domini."</note> Truly, in the "evening" of death, we shall all recognize God’s astonishing Providence toward us. For, as the scripture says:

<margin>Proverbs chapter 20, verse 24.</margin>
*The steps of a man are directed by the Lord; how then can a man understand his own way?* <note>original: "à Domino diriguntur gressus viri, quis autem hominum intelligere potest viam suam?"</note> God leads us with the greatest possible foresight, though often through winding paths and nearly inescapable labyrinths; yet he knows the way by which he leads us out into the lush gardens of heaven. Why then do we complain against this most watchful guide? 

If someone were to begin a journey with a guide <note>The Latin *tabellarius* usually refers to a courier or messenger, but here the author uses it to describe a professional guide or traveler who knows the roads.</note> highly skilled in the routes, and when rough, difficult, and winding paths appear, that person begins to complain and says: "Through what wilderness are you leading me, good man? Unless I am very much mistaken, we have long since lost the way." To this, the guide will promptly respond: "Do not be anxious, my lord, and leave this worry to me. I admit I have led you through some detours; but if we had gone by a straight line, we would have fallen into those inescapable marshes. Trust me; I will lead you so that you will not regret having me as a companion." A path that is well-trodden and safe is never too long or too harsh for anyone. 

This is how divine Providence leads us: we must indeed walk through frequent twists and various turns of the road, but why are we angry at the best of guides? As long as the way is secure, what does it matter if it is rough?

Here is a thought full of comfort: God does not govern us the way a prince governs a province, a King a kingdom, or the Pope <note>original: "summus Pontifex," literally the "Supreme Pontiff," the head of the Catholic Church.</note> the Christian World—all of whom require the labor of many others. So many Archbishops, so many Bishops, and so many other sacred officials relieve the cares of the Pope. Kings have viceroys, princes, lords <note>original: "dynastæ," referring to local rulers or powerful nobles.</note>, counselors, and senators, among whom they divide the burdens of their government. It is not so with God; He governs the whole universe with the same providence by which He governs each individual. Thus, He embraces every single person with a special care, just as He embraces everyone with a general care. *In every place the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil: The Lord looks upon the ways of man, and considers all his steps.*

Would that we might plunge ourselves with a most free leap into the abyss of this most unique and plainly fatherly providence. Let each person promise themselves with the greatest security: *The Lord is concerned for me; the Lord rules me and nothing shall be wanting to me.* Indeed, if we love tranquility of soul—if we desire to trust in God and to obey the divine will in all things—let us keep this divine providence constantly before our eyes. We shall be all the more devoted to the divine will as we become more trusting in divine providence.

## CHAPTER X.

->*How great, nevertheless, is the distrust of many men toward God.*<-

Christ corrected nothing more frequently, and nothing more sharply, in his disciples than distrust. For this reason, he often called them "men of little faith," <note>original: "modicæ fidei"</note> "slow of heart," <note>original: "tardos corde"</note> and an "unbelieving and perverse generation." This best of teachers tried various means so that his followers might unlearn their distrust. For what was the purpose of the Lord’s sleep in the boat, that shortage of bread, that inquiry regarding the provisions to be carried into the wilderness, or Peter’s faltering in the waters? <note>These refer to biblical episodes where the disciples' faith was tested: the storm on the Sea of Galilee, the miraculous feeding of the multitudes, and Peter attempting to walk on water.</note> Distrust was being set forth to be unlearned; and this is the meaning of those words: *You of little faith, why did you doubt?* It was as if that wisest teacher had said: "Are you then so slow to learn that you cannot grasp this first and most necessary lesson?"

Distrust spreads itself into various forms. There are those who distrust God because they think He is too indulgent toward His enemies and gives them free rein <note>original: "laxare omnes habenas," literally "loosening all the reins."</note>. Others distrust that they will obtain from God what they ask for, especially if they are pressed by the pangs of conscience for sins committed in the past, fearing that God might deny pardon even to those who seek it. Others distrust God, fearing perhaps that He might withhold the necessities of life. This triple kind of distrust, by a most direct deception, leads most men away from...

### BOOK V

...never sets out to do anything without first imploring divine aid.

Long ago, Ambrose complained to Monica, the mother of Augustine, regarding her son Augustine, that he trusted too much in his own intellect. Augustine did not become wise until he corrected this self-confidence. <margin>Augustine, *Soliloquies*, chapter 15.</margin> He even confessed this about himself: "I believed," he says, "that I was sufficient through myself, and I did not see that you were ruling me, until you withdrew from me a little while; then I immediately fell into myself, and I saw and I knew." <note>Augustine often wrote about the "fall" into self-reliance as a source of spiritual blindness.</note>

Just as it is a fault to trust in intellect, prudence, or one’s own skill, so it is also a fault to trust in one’s own physical power. The Emperor Maximus <note>Usually identified as Maximinus Thrax, a Roman emperor known for his legendary giant stature and strength.</note> was of such great size and strength (as Capitolinus <note>One of the traditional authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> reports) that he used his wife’s bracelet as a ring. Someone in a theater once sang these little Greek verses <note>The source provides these in Latin, though it identifies them as Greek in origin.</note> to him:

> *The elephant is great, and yet it is killed,*
> *The lion is strong, and yet it is killed,*
> *The tiger is terrible, and yet it is killed;*
> *Beware of the many, if you do not fear the individuals.*

Let no one trust in their strength, no one in their skill, no one in their lineage and wealth, and no one in their education and wisdom, for all these things collapse at the lightest <margin>Jeremiah, chapter 9, verse 23.</margin> breath. Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches.

## ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL
<meta>catchword: Jonah</meta>

...and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. <note>original: "ne, & ponit carnem brachium suum, & à Domino recedit cor ejus." This is the conclusion of Jeremiah 17:5: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man..."</note> On this point, Origen <note>An early and influential Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for his allegorical interpretations of Scripture.</note> speaks acutely, explaining that passage: *Cursed is the man who hangs upon a tree.* <note>original: "Maledictus homo qui pendet in ligno." This is a reference to Deuteronomy 21:23 and Galatians 3:13.</note> I think, he says, that this is the same sentiment as that other: *Cursed is the man who trusts in man.* <note>original: "Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine."</note> For to hang from a tree is the same as having one's hope suspended from a human being, as if from a fragile trunk.

Hunters are accustomed to set such snares in order to capture an elephant. They saw through the bottom of a tree against which an elephant is accustomed to lean while sleeping, but they leave it standing nonetheless, looking as if it were sound and whole. <note>This reflects a common medieval and ancient belief (found in bestiaries) that elephants had no knees and could only sleep by leaning against trees.</note> When the elephant comes to lie down according to its habit, it leans against the cut tree; thus, both the tree and the beast collapse together with great force. There are countless people who choose "trees" for themselves to lean upon: this one strives most laboriously to please a Prince; that one solicits the favor of a wealthy prelate; another insinuates himself into the friendship of a great nobleman; there are those who pursue the goodwill of others through bribery, and others seek favor in various other ways. O wretched men! You deceive yourselves, and you prepare these things for your own destruction. The trees upon which you think to lean have long since been cut by a hidden wound; when you least expect it, they will suddenly fall, and with them all your confidences.

Jonah the prophet made a small shelter for himself and sat beneath it in the shade; and Jonah rejoiced over the ivy <note>original: "hedera." While the plant in the Book of Jonah is often translated as a "gourd" in English Bibles, the Latin Vulgate uses *hedera*, meaning ivy.</note> with great joy. O, what a joy—how brief and how empty! For this "ivy-apartment" had a double enemy: the Sun and the worm. Thus, in a single day, all this shadowy pleasure vanished. Consider the world for me, and you will find it full of such little shelters; they flourish for a time, but a looming destruction always threatens this "ivy" from various worms. To lean upon human favors—alas, how common and widespread a vice this is! If only religious men did not also wish to forget their own dignity here, and gather the grace and favor of others for themselves through secret efforts. These are little "shelters of shadow" which various worms of envy, disparagement, slander, and finally death gnaw at, scatter, and consume.

There is the servant who has the greatest confidence in his master; in a short time, death snatches the master away, and now, where is the servant's entire shelter? Another relies on a wealthy and powerful patron; the patron dies, or his own wealth and power are diminished, and so this man’s ivy has already withered. Children often believe themselves remarkably defended by the authority, offices, and dignity of their parents; suddenly God takes away this shelter, and now the wretched children, contrary to what they had hoped, are scorched by the sun because their "house of ivy" has perished. In this same way, Haman <note>original: "Ama." A reference to Haman, the antagonist of the Book of Esther.</note>, that "eye" of Ahasuerus <note>original: "Assueri." # BOOK V.

...judgment from the Lord goes out for each man <note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing a thought from the previous page: while men may seem powerful, their ultimate destiny is decided by God.</note>.

Jacob, returning from Mesopotamia to Canaan, when he encountered his brother Esau accompanied by four hundred men, feared for himself as if facing a hostile army, and earnestly implored divine aid. God was present for the one calling, and promised the most abundant help; yet, He sent him away limping. And what kind of help or providence is that, you ask? Jacob implores help, and he is sent away with a weak hip <note>original: "coxa debilis." This refers to the biblical story in Genesis 32 where Jacob wrestles with a mysterious figure (often interpreted as an angel or God) and is struck in the socket of his hip, causing him to limp.</note>. Is this "lending a hand"—to make someone lame? Exactly so; this was truly helping. For there are times when even wounds heal us, and a loss suffered at the right moment is actually a gain, and there are many instances in which we are conquered for our own good. And therefore God sent Jacob away from Him "broken" in this way, so that both he and all of us through him might learn not to trust in ourselves or our own strength, nor even in the strength of others, but to rely on the power and goodness of God alone. But because the healthy man trusts in his health, the strong in his vigor, the literate in his learning, the powerful in his gold, and the wise in his wit—and because the lowly man hopes to be supported by the wealthy, and the weak by the influential—therefore God very wisely takes such things away frequently. He does this so that when the crutches on which we were leaning are gone, we may learn to lean on God alone.

God reduced Gideon's army to a tiny fraction to prove that victory came from divine power, not human numbers.</note>

...I have been delivered by my own strength <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely concluding a thought on the folly of claiming credit for one's own safety.</note>. <margin>1 Kings chapter 20, verse 30</margin>

So much for Benhadad; let him go now and trust in his own strength and that of his people. He inflicts no small injury upon God who casts his eyes toward human help rather than divine aid, and who hopes for more from a meager stream than from the immense ocean.

The excellent King Asa (whom we never remember without pity) possessed great trust in God, if only it had remained constant. God certainly rewarded that trust such that Asa overthrew ten hundred thousand <note>that is, one million</note> soldiers whom the King of Ethiopia had under his banners, in a most illustrious victory. But alas, after so many years of noble deeds, this one instance of trust in human strength destroyed this excellent king. Thus the prophet <note>Hanani the Seer, as recorded in 2 Chronicles 16.</note> spoke openly: "Because you had trust," he said, "in the king of Syria, and not in the Lord your God, therefore the army of the king of Syria has escaped from your hand." <margin>Ecclesiastes chapter 9, verse 2.</margin>
Ecclesiastes says: *“Everything,”* he says, *“happens equally to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the bad; to the clean and the unclean; to the one who offers victims and the one who despises sacrifices.”* <note>original Latin: "Vniversa... æque eveniunt juſto & impio." The author is quoting the Vulgate to illustrate the frustration of seeing the same "luck" befall both good and evil people.</note> To us, these things seem to happen rashly and by chance. In this, the same thing happens to us as to someone who looks at a clock in a tower; he sees the <term>gnomon</term> <note>From the Greek for "one who knows." Here, it refers to the hand or indicator of the clock.</note>, or the hand of the clock, but he does not see the clock itself or the ingenious construction of the gears. He would be a pagan, a child, or a fool who believed that the hand moved by itself, and that not by design but by chance. Citizens <note>Latin: "Homines civici." The author uses "city-dwellers" to mean sophisticated or educated people who understand how machinery works, as opposed to someone "uncivilized" who might think a clock is magic or random.</note> know well that the indicator is not moved by itself, but that the clock mechanism lies hidden behind the wall. Exactly so is the governance of God hidden, but most orderly; we see His "indicator" in all things, but we by no means perceive the admirable craftsmanship of Divine Providence. From this come the foolish thoughts of many, to whom almost everything seems to happen by chance. Those who are wiser think differently; they recognize no "luck" in affairs, since they know that all things are governed most providently by the hand of God.

<margin>Gregory of Nazianzus, letter 63.</margin>
Thus says Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and theologian known as "The Theologian."</note>: *“I, for my part,”* he says, *“have found it a certainty that, before the Supreme Reason, nothing in our affairs is without a reason.”*

This clock of Divine Providence has all the hours of every man marked out, even to the smallest points...

### BOOK V.

If we do not hesitate to trust a clock that has a highly skilled caretaker, what kind of foolishness or madness is it to sometimes accuse that great **Clock of the whole World** of error? <margin>Wisdom chapter 14, verses 3 and 4.</margin>

Aldegundis answered her eagerly: "I ask for this one thing," she said, "that what God wills may happen: my only pleasure is the will of the Lord."

III. Saint Francis Xavier <note>Francis Xavier (1506–1552), a co-founder of the Jesuits and a prolific missionary in Asia.</note>, who was the first from the Society of Jesus <note>original: "Societate IESV"</note> to bring the Gospel of Christ into India and Japan, had so deeply imbued his soul with divine providence that he gave many examples of incredible trust in it. Farewell.

A supreme trust in divine providence persuaded him toward such a great agreement with the divine will. Armed with this trust, he looked toward high things and attempted great deeds. This was the primary pursuit of all the Saints: to know divine providence, to rise from that knowledge to trust, and from trust to pass into a most happy union with the divine will; to grow in this daily, and finally to act so that one's own will might lead into or melt into <note>original: "colliquescere," suggesting a total dissolution of the human will into the divine.</note> the divine. They [Joseph's brothers] said none of these things, but spoke with total wisdom: *What is this,* they say, *that God has done to us?* <note>original: "Quidnam est hoc... quod fecit nobis Deus?" Referring to Genesis 42:28.</note> Whatever error or fraud may have occurred, God did this, and He did it to us; the cause of all these things is the will of God, without whose nod not even a grain of sand falls from a mountain, nor a hair from the head, nor a leaf from a tree, nor a sparrow from the air.

We very often, in the manner of dogs that have been struck, bite the stick or the stone; or we get angry at the pen because of poor writing; or we attribute a mistake in a painting to the brush—and we do not consider the hand of the one throwing, writing, or painting. The hand of God does all these things. Indeed, one must speak and think this way in all things: God disposes, God rules, God does all these things. And so that we may best grasp this way of speaking and thinking, we will provide several examples <term>paradigmata: models or patterns used to illustrate a point</term> taken from the mouths of Christ and the Saints.

### ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL

...by your disposition, or condemn anything in your judgments, because it so pleased **YOU**. Look how gently we are taught not to define limits for divine power, not to scrutinize God’s judgments, nor to examine His decrees, but to rest in this one thing: that it so pleases God. The Savior <term>Servator: a common title for Jesus Christ</term> asserts that it thus pleased the Father, but he does not explain *why* it so pleased Him. Indeed, the cause of the divine will is neither to be assigned nor sought. In the place of a thousand reasons is this: God willed it so. The will of divine providence is the highest standard of justice; nor do its reasons remain consistent unless they are rendered to no man <note>The author suggests that God’s justice remains perfect precisely because He is not accountable to human logic or demands for explanation.</note>.

Therefore, in absolutely all things to be done or omitted, to be fled or endured, follow the example of Christ, O Christian, and say always: *Yes, Father; Yes, Father; Yes, my Father* <note>original: "Ita Pater," a reference to the Latin Vulgate of Matthew 11:26: "Ita Pater: quoniam sic fuit placitum ante te."</note>. Even if this must be repeated a thousand times, or even three thousand times in a single day: *Yes, Father.* And it must be said all the more, and repeated diligently, when adversities press harder, by subjecting your will in all things to His most holy will: *Yes, Father.* 

Pronounce this same thing while waking and sleeping, while healthy, sick, and dying, as if you were saying: Lord, I can deny you nothing; you know. Therefore, just as you wish, just as you dispose, ordain, and permit all things to happen, so let them be; yes, Father, so let it be done even in me, and let nothing happen in me that opposes your most upright and best will even in the slightest. *Yes, Father; so be it both now, and always, and for all eternity.*

God looks toward the end He has proposed for Himself in all things, and He achieves it: we too shall achieve our own end if, having recognized His providence, we always submit our own will to His. ### BOOK V.

Whether by His permission or His active ordaining, one should bear things in prosperity and in adversity alike: in the loss of possessions, in injuries, slanders, reproaches, mockeries, and contempt of oneself; in pains of the body, in anguishes and pressures of the heart; in sorrows, in internal abandonment and calamity, and in any afflictions whatever. One should bear these with a patient and tranquil soul, and praise Him, believing that He both wills and is able to promote one's salvation in all things.

## CHAPTER XII.

### *An Epilogue, or a Compendium of all that has been said in these five books.*

I intend here, kind reader, to provide a concise teaching and to offer a summary and <term>epitome</term> <note>A brief summary or abstract of a larger work.</note> of this instruction on conforming our will with the divine, so that what we desire to be always in the soul may always be before the eyes.

For this reason, we have also added images to illustrate this matter. In each of these, you can see a twin symbol representing both the divine and the human will. A heart encircled by a golden crown presents the **Divine Will** to the eyes; this Will is not only the best and most upright, ruling over all things, but it is also immutable and always perfectly consistent with itself. It has a **Lily** and a **Sword** on either side; for it bestows upon mortals both reward and punishment. 

The **Winged Heart** is the symbol of the human will; it wears a wreath woven of roses and, occasionally, of peacock feathers <note>In the symbolic language of the 17th century, roses represent fleeting earthly joy, while peacock feathers often symbolize vanity and inconstancy.</note>. Our power of willing is variable and inconstant; it is only praiseworthy when it raises itself—by its own wings and desires—toward the heart and the Divine Will; or, at the very least, when it does not resist being raised or drawn upward by a higher power <note>Likely referring to the action of Divine Grace drawing the soul.</note>. The human will is always more happy the more closely it is joined to the Divine.

Another symbol of the Divine Will is the **Sun**, and of the human, the **Heliotrope** <note>original: "Heliotropium" — literally the "sun-turner," usually referring to the sunflower or similar plants that track the sun’s movement. It was a favorite emblem for the soul's devotion to God.</note>. Between the sun and this flower, there is the greatest frie—

It sometimes happens that a mistress of the house <note>original: "materfamilias."</note> finds the heated room <term>hypocaustum: a room heated by an underfloor or wall-heating system, often used as a parlor or dining room in colder climates.</term> warmed more than is proper, and thinks she has entered a bathhouse rather than a dining room. At this, the good woman gets "all in a ferment" <note>original: "tota in fermento," an idiom for being worked up or agitated.</note> and pours out all her bitterness <note>original: "bilem," literally "bile," referring to the medieval medical theory of humors where excess yellow bile caused anger.</note> upon the maidservant. But the maid says: "Do not be indignant, my lady; the master <note>original: "herus," the head of the household.</note> ordered it so." As soon as she hears that the master wished it to be done that way, she restrains her anger and speaks more gently; she learns not to feel the heat, which was otherwise unpleasant. And here is the end of a struggle that would otherwise have been dragged out into a wordy argument. It was worth so much to have given that single response: *The master willed it so.* Let this same thought persuade us to a gentle silence in all adversities, having thought this one thing: *God willed it so* <note>original: "Deus ita voluit."</note>.

And the ancient Fathers called this a great exercise: to receive everything from God's hand, which Job and David performed most perfectly. <margin>Job chapter 1, verse 21.</margin> The former [Job] said: *The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so has it been done; blessed be the name of the Lord.* It is as if he were to say: The Lord lent these things, and did not renounce His ownership; therefore, what is His, He can take back; let Him be blessed, and let thanks be given to Him. <margin>Psalm 33, verse 1.</margin> Nor did King David act differently: *I will bless the Lord,* he said, *at all times,* both in adversity and prosperity, however He has dealt with me. 

This resignation of one's own will to the divine is a work of supreme perfection and sincere love; for the highest degree of friendship is to **WILL** and **NOT WILL** the same things. <note>original: "idem velle et nolle." This phrase is a classical definition of friendship by the Roman historian Sallust, here used to describe the soul’s friendship with God.</note> In this way, a person places all their emotions under the yoke and adapts their whole self to the divine will, and joyfully sings with Blessed Bernard: *My life is in Your will, O Lord.* <margin>St. Bernard, Sermon 14 on the Song of Songs, near the middle.</margin> Jerome, discussing this excellently, says: "God is good, and it is necessary that all things which a good Being does must be good. Is the loss of a husband imposed? I mourn what has happened: but because it so pleases the Lord, I will endure it with a level mind. An only son is snatched away—"

### III. The BENEFITS of a Human Will Conformed to the Divine.

I will put it briefly: A human will that agrees with the divine in all things is a full suit of armor <note>original: "panoplia"; a complete set of armor for a soldier, covering the whole body.</note> for all the virtues. From this armory, weapons are surely supplied against every kind of misfortune. Indeed, anyone who has joined <note>original: "agglutinavit"; literally, "glued" or "fastened."</note> his will to the divine will, whatever sad or terrifying thing happens in nature, looking down upon it with a calm mind, will repeat this one phrase: Let the will of the Lord be done. <note>original: "Fiat voluntas Domini," a central petition from the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:10).</note> If his wealth is snatched away or his house burns down, he will say: Let the will of the Lord be done. If he is plagued by diseases, shaken by pains, or torn by torments, even then he will cry out: Let the will of the Lord be done. If he is stripped of all honor and harassed by countless insults, he will still not stop saying: Let the will of the Lord be done. Though all men may trouble him and all demons insult him; though the sky should fall, the world perish, and the gates of hell open, he will still shout: Let the will of the Lord be done. In the greatest disasters, his greatest comfort is to be able to say: "It has pleased the Lord so; God wills this."

When Bion <note>Bion of Borysthenes (c. 325–250 BC), a Greek philosopher known for his witty sayings and his transition from the Academy to Cynicism and finally to a more relaxed philosophy.</note> was asked who seemed to be the most anxious person in life, he replied: "In my opinion, it is the one who desires to be most successful in the greatest affairs; for he is strangled by a thousand cares in order to achieve...

Now, what greater solace <note>original: "solatium"</note> can there be anywhere in this world than to most lovingly embrace the most holy will of God in all things? Let us only apply reason to our difficulties and submit our own will to the divine will in everything; by this one method, hard things can most easily be softened, narrow things widened, and heavy burdens can weigh less upon those who bear them skillfully. All things become both easy and pleasant for us, provided we surrender ourselves to every judgment of God.

Second. *God's singular guidance in all things.* For he who so generously entrusts himself entirely to the divine will—desiring nothing more ardently than to both know and follow it in all things—the life of such a man is certainly so tempered and ruled by God in every single moment that he sees what God wants in almost everything, and finds that all things turn toward his own good. This is asserted concerning Joseph, the viceroy of Egypt:

It happens exactly like this: a man devoted and dedicated to the divine will is singularly guided by the divine hand in all his actions, and is directed toward understanding and carrying out the will of God.

Fourthly. *A happy management of one's own salvation and that of others.* He who clings stubbornly to his own opinion and purpose, since he does not easily allow himself to be bent toward anything else, must necessarily block many paths for himself and cut off opportunities for doing right. <note>The left edge of the page is slightly cropped; the bracketed letters are reconstructed from context.</note> [H]uman evil is one's **own will** <note>original: "voluntas propria"</note>, when it does not consent with the divine will. Since the **intellect** and the **will** are joined by the tightest bond of friendship, it is easy—if the will burns with a desire for any certain thing—for the intellect to be led not only into consenting, but even into approving of what the will desires. For the intellect is like a **Legal Scholar** <note>original: "Iureconsultus"; a specialist in law who provides legal opinions.</note> who, having been corrupted by flatteries and bribes, explains the laws not according to the intent of the lawmaker, but according to the wish of the one paying him. <margin>Anselm, *Similitudes*, chapter 8.</margin>
Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher known as the father of Scholasticism.</note> speaks wisely concerning one's own evil will: "God alone," he says, "must want whatever He wants by His own will, such that He has no other will above Him to follow. Therefore, when a man wants something through his **own will**, he takes away, as it were, God’s own crown. For just as a crown belongs to the King alone, so one’s own will belongs to God alone; and just as one would most severely injure a King by taking away his crown, so a man offends God greatly when he snatches for himself what belongs to God." But just as God’s own will is the fountain and origin of all good, so man’s own will is the beginning of all evil. It is exactly so: no obstacle is missing where one's own will is present; there are no hurdles where a singular <note>Meaning a will that acts alone or in isolation from God.</note> will falters.

Ah, why do we miserable ones resist, so that we do not...

### V. *Aids for Conforming the Human Will with the Divine.*

The primary place here is held by the knowledge of divine providence and, arising from this, a constant trust in God. Serious meditation on God’s providence is the sole remedy against those countless and most foolish anxieties of men. For indeed, what is more foolish than not to hope for the smallest things from the "Best and Greatest" God, <note>original: "Deo optimo Maximo," a common Latin formula for God, often abbreviated as D.O.M.</note> who gives the greatest things of His own accord? That saying of Job must be repeated and drummed in a thousand times: <margin>Job chapter 5, verse 6.</margin> "Nothing on earth happens without a cause—nothing, nothing—not even the smallest of things." This hand of eternal providence...

He [God] directs all things with the greatest wisdom. Evils do not happen to us by chance, nor do they spring from the ground like weeds. All things come from on high. That which some imagine to be "fortune," we recognize as the highest providence of God. The counsels of divine providence are indeed hidden, but they are most just; the progression of events directed by divine providence is secret, but it is most certain.

<margin>Proverbs 16:33</margin>
The lots are cast into the lap, but they are regulated by the Lord. <note>original: "Sortes mittuntur in sinum, sed à Domino temperantur." Yet, the fact that some are called to wealth or to the seizing of honors over others is not a matter of fortune, but of the providence of God. He regulates everything—even the very smallest things—in such a way that for some, a lot of happiness falls to them, while others miss out; this happens not by chance, but by God's most certain decree.

<margin>Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 96.</margin>

He constantly turns this over in his mind: that God is at once the wisest governor, the most powerful king, and the best father. As the governor, He knows most providently; as the king, He is able to act most effectively; and as the father, He wills most lovingly both to supply true goods and to turn away true evils.

<header>CONCERNING THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL</header>

...[once he] has learned to recognize Providence, he will not hesitate to commit himself to it. Moreover, for one who has surrendered himself to God in this manner, it will be very easy to yield most deeply to the law and authority of the divine will. His mind will be so composed that it aims for the one and only will of God in all things. Not only will he no longer wish for or reject anything except what God wills or does not will, but even if he were permitted to disagree with God’s will, he would nonetheless never desire to want or not want anything other than what he knew pleased the divine will.

This is what Catherine of Siena <note>St. Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), a mystic and Doctor of the Church known for her "Dialogue" on spiritual providence</note> most rightly advises: that those who are seriously devoted to virtue should build a secret chamber of the **DIVINE WILL** within their own breast. They should shut themselves away here, dwell in it perpetually, and never peer out with a curious eye, nor reach out with a straying hand, nor step out with a wandering foot. Rather, just as a bee stays in its hive, or as a gem remains fixed in its setting <note>original: "monili," referring to a necklace or jewel-piece</note>, so should they persist most constantly in the divine will. He who wholeheartedly devotes himself entirely to the divine will quickly attains the sum of all virtues.

[Antiochus] stretched out [his hand] to him; but Popilius, in turn, refused to stretch out his own. With a face set in solemn majesty, he said: "Let us set aside private friendship; public matters must now be cared for." And at once he brought forth the decree of the senate, by which the king was ordered either not to enter Egypt or to have war with the Roman people. When Antiochus read the tablets sent by the senate, he said he would confer with his friends. To him, Popilius replied: "The business does not allow for delay; all hesitation must be removed." And at the same time, with a rod which he was carrying in his hand, he marked the pavement, drawing a circle in it, and said: "Before you step out of this circle, give me the answer that I am to bring back to the senate." You would have believed not that an envoy was speaking, but that the Senate House <note>original: "curiam," referring to the Roman Curia where the Senate met</note> itself was placed before your eyes. For the king immediately affirmed that it would be done, so that Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy VI, the ruler of Egypt whom Rome was protecting</note> would have no further cause to complain about him. And only then did Popilius grasp his hand as that of an ally: thus in the same moment he terrified the king of Syria and protected the king of Egypt.

Almost the same thing happens to us as happened to Antiochus; we wish to be friends with God, but we do not like to cross over into God's will. Therefore, the Son, sent as an envoy into the world <note>original: "Orbem," meaning the world or the orb of the earth</note> by the Father, drawing the circle of the divine will around us, says: *Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of the Father.* Look, my friend <note>original: "mi homo," a familiar, direct address to the reader</note>, you are enclosed in this circle, and you shall not step out before you have said whether [you submit] to the judgment...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "Dei" indicates the next page begins with "of God."</meta>

<summary>The author recounts the famous historical incident of the "line in the sand" drawn by Roman envoy Popilius to illustrate how God's will demands an immediate and total decision from the believer.</summary>
<keywords>Popilius, Antiochus, Egypt, Divine Will, obedience, Roman Senate, Matthew 7:21, spiritual surrender</keywords>

# ON THE CONFORMITY OF THE WILL
<note>original: "DE CONF. VOLVNT." abbreviated from "De Conformitate Voluntatis." This is likely from the works of Jeremias Drexel, a 17th-century Jesuit writer.</note>

<margin>
1 John
chapter 2,
verse 17.
</margin>
Whether you wish to surrender yourself to God or live according to your own pleasures. If peace is dear to your heart, if you do not wish to be an enemy of the Divine <note>original: "Numinis," a Latin term for divine power or a deity</note>, if you hate unholy war with God, you will give an answer immediately. Ah, my good Christian, why do you turn back, why do you deliberate, why do you delay? This business hates delay <note>original: "moram odit hoc negotium," a common Latin expression meaning time is of the essence</note>. If you are wise, you will imitate that king <note>Referring to King Antiochus from the previous page, who gave his answer before stepping out of the circle drawn in the sand.</note> and answer most readily: My God, I hand myself over most perfectly and entirely to your most holy will, and I bind myself to it, ready both to act and to suffer, to live and to die, just as you wish. In whatever troubles, even the most heavy, your most upright will shall be my greatest comfort. I now establish this as my one and only rule for both living and dying: **Let the will of the Lord be done, let it be done, let it be done.** <note>original: "Fiat voluntas Domini, fiat, fiat."</note> Though all things be disturbed by various storms, though weapons rage in mutual clashes, though fleets be shattered against fleets, though the courts clamor all day long with lawsuits, and all things be in a tumult of busy efforts—I take this one task upon myself: to compose my whole being according to the one and only will of God. And now I embrace with my innermost heart that most holy oracle: **The world passes away and its lusts: but he who does the will of God, remains** **FOREVER.**

---

->Praise be to God, to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and to all the Holy Angels.<-

<summary>The author concludes the treatise by urging the reader to surrender their personal will to God's will immediately and without hesitation. The text ends with a prayer of total devotion and a citation from the First Epistle of John regarding the eternal nature of doing God's will.</summary>

<keywords>Divine Will, spiritual surrender, peace of heart, 1 John 2:17, perseverance, prayer of surrender, internal peace, spiritual discipline</keywords>

# APPROVAL
<note>original: "APPROBATIO." This is the official permission from the author's religious superiors to publish the work.</note>

->BY THE REVEREND FATHER PROVINCIAL.<-
<note>The "Provincial" is a high-ranking Jesuit official overseeing a specific geographic region, in this case, Upper Germany.</note>

*Having had the five books of the* Sunflower <note>original: "Heliotropii." The sunflower was a popular 17th-century symbol for the soul because it turns its face toward the sun (God) throughout the day.</note> *regarding the* ALIGNMENT *of the human will with the divine—which Father Jeremias Drexel, a Priest of our Society, has written—examined and approved by several theologians of the same Society; I, Gualterus Mundbrot, Provincial Superior of the Society of JESUS throughout Upper Germany, by the power granted to me by our very Reverend Father General Mutio Vitellesco, permit them to be brought to light.*

*In witness of this matter, I have given this signed document to the author, fortified with the seal of my office. At Munich, on the day of the Conversion of St. Paul,*
IN THE YEAR 1627,

->Gualterus Mundbrot.<-
